Chile y México: Unidos en el arte, el diseño y la solidaridad 🇨🇱🤝🇲🇽

¿Sabías que México acudió en ayuda de Chile tras los terremotos de Chillán (1939) y Valdivia? ¿Y que ese apoyo quedó inmortalizado en obras de arte y arquitectura que se pueden encontrar en Santiago y Concepción? De estas acciones y sus alcances expuso el Dr. Rodrigo Vera Manríquez @veramanriquez , en su visita a  la Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, UNAM, el pasado 6 de octubre.

El director del Instituto de Historia y Patrimonio del Depto. de Diseño de la Facultad de Arquitectura y Urbanismo de la Universidad de Chile se presentó en el Aula Enrique del Moral de la Facultad de Arquitectura UNAM. Allí, dictó la conferencia “El Plan chileno-mexicano de cooperación fraternal (1960-1964): arquitectura, arte y diseño para la fraternidad de dos pueblos”, en la hizo una revisión histórica y estética de las donaciones y aportes artísticos y culturales brindados por México a Chile, durante la reconstrucción del país tras los terremotos de Chillán y Valdivia. 

¿Qué obras surgieron en estos períodos?

📍 “Presencia de América Latina” de Jorge González Camarena, ubicado en la Casa del Arte de la U. de Concepción, Concepción. (Foto 1)
📍 “De México a Chile” de Xavier Guerrero, mural en la Escuela República de México. (Foto 5). 
📍 “Muerte al Invasor” de David Alfaro Siqueiros, mural en la Biblioteca Pedro Aguirre Cerda, Santiago. ( Foto 8)
📍 “Fraternidad de dos pueblos indoamericanos”. Diseña por Juan O’Gorman y ejecutada por María Martner. Emplazada en el cerro San Cristóbal, Santiago.
📍El Club México de boxeo de Santiago.
📍El Club México de Boxeo de Osorno: con murales del artista mexicano Tomás Parra y la participación de artistas chilenos como María Martner y Nemesio Antúnez.

La conferencia, organizada por el Laboratorio Editorial de Arquitectura UNAM, fue parte de las actividades de Chile en México, realizadas con el apoyo del Área de Diseño del Ministerio de las Culturas, las Artes y el Patrimonio de Chile, que incluyeron la inauguración de la exposición Visión y Tradición, en el marco de @designweekmex

An Ocean of Love by Anthea Amore @antheaamoreceramics

An Ocean of Love draws on ancient mythology in which the oyster is associated with Aphrodite, goddess of love and beauty. The form becomes a vessel for divine femininity, creation, and desire, holding space for tenderness and strength. Oyster shells evoke protection and emergence, suggesting love as something guarded and generative. The shell’s layered, spiraling form speaks to growth shaped by experience; how pressure and irritation gives rise to something precious. The work invites viewers to reflect on love’s origins; born of the sea, shaped by time, and endlessly renewed.

In the September issue of ArtReview, Adeline Chia explores the work of Indonesian collective Taring Padi, who consider themselves activists first and artists second. Clive Chijioke Nwonka examines the redevelopment of London’s Hackney Wick and the effects of enlisting cultural institutions in such endeavours. Alexandra Symons-Sutcliffe discusses Kate Millett’s Terminal Piece (1972), made in response to the highly publicised murder of an American teenage girl. Elsewhere, Martin Herbert considers how Jasper Johns’s paintings often hide more than they reveal; Nicole Kaack explores how Sophie Becker’s ventriloquism performances question who is really in charge; Zoë Hopkins traces the rich history of black graphic scores, making the case that Black musical culture has always also been a visual culture; and Emily McDermott speaks with poet Ana María Caballero about what art is — and what AI isn’t.

Plus, reviews from around the world, including London, New York, Barcelona, Antananarivo, and more...

#LaMasíaGallery No puedes perderte la exposición de @quimgordun "Revelarse (显露)" en La Masía Gallery de Barcelona, situada la segunda planta de la flagship de @nudeproject, la tercera exposición comisariada por Urvanity Projects.⁠
⁠
Un cuadro no muestra todo lo que contiene. A veces su fuerza está en cómo los elementos se cubren, se ocupan o se desplazan entre sí. En la obra de Quim Gordun, la imagen va unida a la lógica del camuflaje y a la composición dinámica. El fondo interviene en la figura: en lo que queda dentro del cuerpo, entre los rasgos, entre los elementos de la composición. Es ahí donde la imagen se mantiene en proceso de revelarse. Se sostiene en ese punto donde empieza a hacerse evidente, firme incluso cuando solo se deja ver parcialmente.⁠
⁠
Esta exposición reúne obras realizadas entre 2025 y 2026, un periodo en el que esa forma de revelación aparece de maneras distintas. Algunas piezas conservan todavía una relación más directa con el paisaje o la estructura compositiva; otras quedan más frontales, más suspendidas. En todas ellas, sin embargo, late una misma intuición: la imagen no se entrega del todo.⁠
⁠
⁠
📍Carrer dels Boters, 6, Barcelona⁠

Thanks to the generosity of our Father's Day market community and the extraordinary matching donation from Applecross Rotary, $10,000 is on its way to Nepal flood victims. 💛

On Sunday 6 September, the generous people who attended our Father's Day Perth Makers Market at Goolugatup Heathcote donated a remarkable $5,000 through parking donations to the RAWCS Nepal Flooding Disaster Relief Fund — money that will go directly to individuals, families and communities devastated by the recent flooding disaster in Nepal.

And then our wonderful Applecross Rotary volunteers did something extraordinary. They contributed another $5,000, bringing the total contribution to $10,000!

Rotary member Ken Williams, who was volunteering on the day, said it best.

"When people heard about what we were raising the funds for they immediately doubled their donations. It was so great to see the generosity of the community."

To every single person who parked at Goolugatup Heathcote on Sunday and made a donation — thank you. You came to celebrate Father's Day, browse local handmade stalls and enjoy a day by the river, and in doing so you helped change lives on the other side of the world. That is the kind of community we are so proud to be part of.

And to the Applecross Rotary volunteers who give up their time at every single Perth Makers Market event and then went above and beyond to match your generosity — we cannot thank you enough. 💛

To find out more about RAWCS and the Nepal Flooding Disaster Relief Fund or to make a personal donation visit rawcs.org.au.

Tide Dwellers by Jan Brown @janbrownmetalart

Inspired by limpets, small marine creatures clinging firmly to coastal rocks. Limpets play an important role in 
maintaining healthy ocean ecosystems, grazing on algae, preventing overgrowth and creating space for other marine life to thrive. Hand-woven copper wire, these sculptures evoke the strength and resilience of these remarkable creatures. Fragments of found beach rope, woven into selected pieces, reference ghost nets and marine debris drifting through our oceans. Their groupings suggest shelter, connection and coexistence. Reflecting the resilience of coastal communities and the delicate balance sustaining life within our shared environment.

caption:
Medusa by Angus Wilson

Discarded steel transforming industrial remnants into a form that echoes both growth and ruin. The tree built from salvaged material marked by wear, corrosion and stress, allowing the history of the steel to remain visible. Scars speak of previous use and abandonment, becoming part of the work rather than something to be hidden. Twisted branches rise and writhe toward the sky, evoking movement, tension and defiance. Their contorted forms suggest struggle as much as growth, as if the tree has adapted to harsh conditions and continues reaching upward despite them.

Buoy'n'Sea by Colin Dray @coldray

This body of nine sculptures investigates buoyancy, flotation and propulsion in marine environments, tracing how different bodies move through water. Fish regulate buoyancy via swim bladders; jellyfish drift in an almost weightless suspension. Humans, by contrast, rely on displaced or trapped air, weighted belts and engineered vessels. Propulsion emerges through propellers, fins, paddles, or jets of water. Each work fuses these natural and mechanical strategies, reflecting shared principles that allow organisms and machines to float, balance and move through the sea. Humans must respect and protect marine life.

Byte Catch by The Southport School and Melissa Ballard @tss_thesouthportschool

Much like a pod of dolphins, TSS boys draw on shared intelligence and collective strength through teamwork. 
Care and intergenerational connection are fostered through traditions and rituals that cultivate purpose and 
belonging. Technological artefacts and their by-products permeate every layer of contemporary life and now present new challenges. PFAS, plastic waste, and underwater data farms exemplify the unintended environmental and societal consequences of technological advancement. Through this work, the school community reflects on these challenges, raising awareness and inviting consideration of possible pathways toward a thriving and sustainable future.

Hay imágenes que no representan una realidad, sino que emergen desde territorios más profundos, entre la memoria, el deseo y la imaginación. En Tetramorfo, Laia García presenta un nuevo cuerpo de trabajo donde la figura humana se transforma en criaturas, símbolos, formas orgánicas y presencias ambiguas que parecen existir en un estado continuo de mutación.⁠
⁠
Situada entre la figuración y la abstracción, su pintura explora la forma como espacio de transformación. A través del gesto, el color y la densidad de la materia, cada obra se convierte en una experiencia sensorial donde lo conocido y lo extraño conviven, invitando al espectador a permanecer en la incertidumbre y a contemplar aquello que todavía se resiste a ser nombrado.⁠

Art Jakarta is pleased to announce that Nata-Citta Art Space (N-CAS) ISI Bali returns to AJX.

AJX is a collaboration between Art Jakarta and various local and international institutions to showcase presentations that offer insights into the region’s current flair.

Nata-Citta Art Space (N-CAS) ISI Bali, a public space for art and design, as well as a platform for diverse expressions of contemporary art, is now advancing with a new vision since 2021. This vision goes beyond being merely an exhibition venue; it is also a laboratory of appreciation and a center of artistic creativity, dedicated to talented students, lecturers, and professional artists. Various international art events have marked the presence of N-CAS, such as the Bali-Bhuwana Rupa International Exhibition since 2021, the Bali-Global Arts Maps Exhibition (B-GAME) since 2024, the Bali Megarupa Exhibition since 2023, and the Bali Kandarupa Exhibition in 2025. N-CAS has become known as a creative hub for numerous international artists, including those from South Korea, Japan, the Netherlands, France, Australia, Malaysia, and Singapore.

Arches at Play by Renee Kire @reneekire

Arches at Play explores form and colour through experimentation and spatial curiosity. The arches engage with one another and their surroundings. Some stand upright, while others lean, respond to neighbouring forms, or seem on the verge of toppling, suggesting movement and balance. The work invites viewers to navigate the space with curiosity, considering the relationships between objects, their surroundings, and themselves. Through scale and spatial arrangement, simple forms become active participants in shaping our experience of the environment.

It's hard to believe that a month has already passed since Pickathon and that summer is quickly drawing to a close. The music, laughter, and spirit of the weekend is still resounding through my heart, and I'm so honored to have had the chance to once again be a part of the magic and fun on the farm. I had such a ribbiting time hanging out in Captain Coyote's Frog Bog taking care of the Lily Pad Post Office and serving as typist and typewriter teacher alike, and I hope that all around the world the beautiful Lily Pad Postcards people created are finding their way to family, friends, and loved ones. It's such an incredible feeling to have the opportunity to be The Traveling Typist, to share that spark of typewriter joy with spirits both young and old, and I'll never tire of hearing  nimble fingers typing away and channeling their inner creativity. 

I want to give a huge thank you to everyone who stopped by the Lily Pad Post Office, both to create their own Lily Pad Postcard and to try out writing on a typewriter. For me being The Traveling Typist is about so much more than just writing, it's about cultivating that incredible sense of community, joy, and creativity that typewriters inspire. I also want to thank @pickathon and @pickathoncoyote for having me, @redyarnpdx for his amazing work in helping to plan and bring Frog Bog to life, and to everyone else at Pickathon who helped make the weekend magical.

Reciprocity by Kayla Finlayson @kayla.finlayson

Reciprocity is a large-scale, hand-built ceramic sculpture modelled on a freshwater mussel native to the Tweed Valley river system. It developed after the 2022 floods, when great numbers of Cucumerunio Novahollandiae shells were exposed along the riverbed on Ngarakwal Country, prompting reflection on cultural history, environmental fragility and time. The event also marked Finlayson’s personal reconnection to place and 
regaining stability with her daughters following displacement. By enlarging this often-overlooked keystone species to monumental scale, she highlights ecological interdependence and advocates for habitat 
conservation, education and deeper connection to Country.

#Installation ¿Qué pasaría si el Casal Solleric se hundiera lentamente bajo el mar? En “Había en el fondo del mar”, @nuriamora convierte el edificio en un escenario submarino poblado por pecios, tesoros y formas híbridas que parecen emerger de un naufragio imaginario. EL KHAT القات (@elkhatmusic) in the Galaxy Barn at @pickathon.

The Berlin-based trio was formed in Jaffa, the members descendents of the Yemeni diaspora. Although they seem to consider themselves nationless, they grew up part of a Yemeni-Jewish culture being introduced to music through the synagogue. More than a dozen years ago, frontman Eyal El Wahab played cello for Jerusalem Andalusian Orchestra performing ancient music from North Africa and Europe.

Eyal's story reads like one of conflicted identity that's easy to relate to. While European and American Jews are universally legitimized, the idea of being Arab and Jewish has been framed as being fundamentally at odds with itself. After coming across a Dust To Digital comp of Yemeni traditional music, Eyal finally discovered something he felt connected to on a deeper level. He learned Arabic and began exploring sounds from his mother land while incorporating outside elements like psych rock. The vocalist/multi-instrumentalist  plays what have been referred to as "junkyard" instruments, which he crafts from discarded wood, metal, plastic, and found objects. Simplicity and polyrythms are core elements of what El Khat create.

Their live performances are mesmerizing, engaging affairs with the members often entering the crowd to dance with the audience. Their two Pickathon sets were no different. El Khat performances showcase their heritage filtered through a uniquely modern yet timeless lens. If they can be reduced to one singular concept, it would be the celebration of freedom and connection.

Collapsing sign-systems masquerading as coherence, a semiotic clot wherein art is strangled by its own exhausted referents. Shown as sculpture, really a schema in free fall, institutionalised legibility forced into 
silhouettes after they have lost their capacity to mean. Orchestrated semiotic implosion of commodified vitality, the vernacular of packaging masquerades as ecological detritus, a dialogic tension between the "JUICE" of lore

appropriation, transforming it into a signifier of depleted potency, beached & bound on the littoral edge.

Emergency Housing by Russell Solomon @rustywiresculptures

Emergency Housing, Russell Solomon’s most recent series of small scale sculptures, connects the hermit 
crab's global environmental and housing crisis with the human environment and housing crisis. Using found,
recycled and repurposed plastics coupled with whimsical, witty titles for each element of the collective installation the work is a humorous, ostentatious representation of the hermit crabs using discarded plastics as their shells/homes. The work visualises a shared, urgent reality of insecure existence caused by unchecked systems of commodification and environmental destruction.

Ngagambi is a Butherim Gaurimah, a totemic story carried through generations by narrative and interaction. The Giant Black Dingo’s songline begins at Point Danger and travels across the continent, traversing many Nations and Law systems. Installed as three separate sculptural elements, the work appears fragmented when encountered individually. Only from a specific vantage point do the forms align to reveal Ngagambi’s full silhouette. Both protector and punisher, Ngagambi embodies the balance of Law, inviting reflection on responsibility, perspective, and the enduring governance embedded within Country

Keelbone by Chainsaw Newton @chainsawnewton

Keelbone, a timber sculpture formed of reclaimed timber beams, assembled like a spine drawn from the tide. Its rhythym of ribs echoes marine animals- fish, trilobite, whale -while the arc and taper recall hull kee and oar. Weathered cuts and tool marks remain visible, carrying the labour and former lives of the wood. Positioned low to the sand the work sits between beach and shore suggesting a vessel at rest where biology and boat-building meet. Memory, wind, shoreline and time shape its quiet presence here.

Rising from the shifting sands of Currumbin Beach, a large series of repetitive hands mark the dawn of a new era. In the installation "The Rise of AI", weathered 3D Printed forms serve as a physical metaphor for a changing world. This work explores the thinning line between human touch and artificial intelligence, asking: as technology mimics us, will it support our future or replace the hands that created it?

Marine Harp by Damien Ricketson @damien.curiousnoise 

Marine Harp is an installation of fishing rods transforming wave motion into gentle tones. A cluster of fishing rods jut from the shallows of the beach, curved taut with a valuable catch: the sound of the sea. As water caresses the fishing line like the bow of a cello drawn across its string, ocean waves become sound waves surging mournfully with the swell. This otherworldly string orchestra, played entirely by the ocean, catches an ancient dialogue between sea and land.

Between Worlds by Amy Thai @amythai.art

'Between Worlds' is cast in the round, no fixed front, no single reading. From one angle, pure abstraction: twisting ribbons of bronze folding through negative space. Move around the work and two ethereal figures emerge, limbs, torsos, the curve of a shoulder, then dissolve again. The forms draw from nature: its flux, its transience. The figures do not merge. They interlock, each retaining its own momentum. The patina shifts from gold to deep green. Two figures from separate worlds, momentarily held together by the place where they touch.

North Carolina trio, SETTING (@settingsounds) played their first set at this year's @pickathon music festival during the daytime on the Windmill stage. Comprised of multi-instrumentalists Nathan Bowles, Jaime Fennelly, and Joe Westerlund, the group builds and evolves their live compositions through improvisation. The same is true with their studio efforts. Even a 90 second clip on this post won't provide an accurate sample of what they do; as each tune is born from luminiferous ether, sprouting life while mutating and slipping dimensions.

Westerlund and Bowles handle the rhythm section, blending the standard drums and percussion, respectively, while incorporating everything from zither and metalaphone to banjo. It can seem like a very kitchen sink approach, but they have a handle on their tools. New timbres and colors are thrown into the mix and allowed to meld in as the sonics churn like spin art.

Behind the keys, Bowles might pick up a bow from his station to run across the edge of a ride cymbal. Something is always happening to make the audience curious about what's going on up there. They are in front of the curtain, so to speak, creating without shield, yet bewildering in their process of mixing potions and conjuring magic right in front of you.

Fennelly sits behind an arrangement of both modern and analog synthesizers, shaping, guiding, and reacting to the pieces brought forth by his collaborators while pulling from the atmosphere around him. Known for blending past and future technologies with harmonium, Jaime embodies the concept of the organic and electronic coming together and merging in surprising and unexpected ways.

I spoke to Bowles a bit, after noticing him during Mary Halvorson's set. He confirmed that, despite their fluidity, he and his cohorts were creating on the fly out there. He wasn't offended by my reference to Los Angeles quartet, SML, a comparison I only make due to their ability to be uncategorizeable. Like SML, Setting can morph and shift their sound into any direction without notice, from the earthy and percussive to the most tripped-out psychedelic, kosmiche music, or glitchy interstellar pulsation.

Big Bang Cluster by Andre Sardone @andre.sardone.art

This ‘Big Bang’ series is the culmination of a structural form that has evolved over many years. At its core is a central hub from which shafts radiate outward, a form that echoes both the delicate structure of a dandelion 
and the primordial explosion of the Big Bang itself, matter and energy dispersing endlessly from a single point of origin. This recurring form has been revisited and reimagined over time in Andre’s arts practice, realised in a range of materials and scales, from intimate, hand-held works to monumental sculptural statements.

Morning Star by Harmony Linthorne @harmonylinthorne.art

Morning Star is a reflective, site-responsive work that explores transformation and embodied perception within
shared space. Constructed from mirrored and industrial materials, the work fragments light, landscape, and viewers, producing shifting encounters that move between attraction and disorientation. 
Drawing on celestial forms and ornamental excess, Morning Star encourages playful engagement while 
prompting moments of self-awareness and vulnerability. Situated against the landscape, the work activates its surroundings, using reflection and distortion to blur boundaries between object and body, inviting audiences to consider their presence within an ever-changing environment.

Inspired by the ethereal presence of Migaloo, this sculpture honors the white whale’s deep connection to our Gold Coast community. To mirror his rare, ivory form, I have meticulously arranged thousands of white seashells into rhythmic, textured patterns. The use of white-on-white highlights the purity of the ocean and the 
fragility of marine life. By ethically utilizing the sea’s own natural architecture to depict its most famous traveler, I hope to create a lasting bond between the viewer and the majestic, fleeting spirit of the whale.

I am delighted, honoured and grateful to receive the 2026 Swell Sculpture Festival Jennie Neumann Emerging Artist Award for my piece, Reflections.
I want to thank all the Swell staff for all the hard work putting the event on, the volunteers helping me install, and all my friends and family who contributed to making it happen. I’d also like to extend my gratitude to the Neumann family for sponsoring this award 🙏

Reflections invites participants to move through and around the structure, encountering their own image as it fragments and multiplies. The work explores the human need to reflect on the past while remaining oriented toward what lies ahead. While reflection is essential for growth, lingering too long can obstruct forward momentum. By framing both the participant and the surrounding landscape, Reflections balances inward contemplation with outward projection, encouraging awareness of self, context, and future direction

Call of the Theropods by Dave Hickson

Call of the Theropods is a vibrant, large-scale sculpture representing avian life throughout history. Its imposing 
size seeks to dissolve the boundaries between the human and bird kingdoms. An integrated speaker broadcasts the songs of numerous Australian birds, inviting visitors to identify these calls themselves or by using the fantastic Merlin Bird ID App. The app was developed by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology at Cornell University. You are encouraged to contribute to this scientific community by uploading bird recordings to enhance the app’s database.

@kaecee.fitzgerlad @natalie.haskell @living_islands_research_lab

This project explores more-than-human design through a sculptural installation made from 3D-printed clay, oyster calcium carbonate, reclaimed shells, and translucent PETG. It commemorates living with oysters, 
proposing design as an ethical relationship between humans and nonhuman life. Inspired by oyster reefs, the work embeds biological history into form while contrasting human infrastructure with light as a symbol of fragility and permeability. After the exhibition, the structure is submerged, becoming a marine habitat and 
ecological participant.

Lumie, The Desert Hopper of Light by Devorah Ungerleider @devorah_creates

Lumie emerges as a response to a fragmented world, offering a moment of pause and recognition. Constructed from hand-painted canvases inspired by human skin tones, precious metals, and everyday cosmetics, the sculpture’s quilted surface unites many parts into a single form. Community-written wishes for healing, peace, and connection mark Lumie’s legs like living tattoos. Inspired by the desert hare, Lumie stands as a quiet guardian, alert, intuitive, and luminous, reminding us that beneath our differences, we share the same hopes.

Amaranth is an interactive installation. Rising from a perforated aluminium base, a stem arches overhead to 
support a large sculptural bloom. This botanical-industrial hybrid invites visitors to stand beneath its canopy, encouraging curiosity and contemplation. Light radiates from a central orb, travelling through the stem to illuminate the bloom, casting ethereal shadows and creating an immersive experience for all who gather beneath.

A quick parking update for our Father's Day Market on Sunday 6 September. 🚗

As many of you may know, the Heathcote Lowerlands is currently undergoing an exciting redevelopment by the City of Melville. While we love seeing this beautiful space get the upgrade it deserves, due to delays in construction it does mean parking will look a little different at our Father's Day Market this Sunday. 

Here is what you need to know:

🅿️ Lowerlands parking will be available as usual — just at a reduced capacity for this event only.

🕐 Come later in the day if you would like a quieter experience and easier parking. Our markets are typically busiest in the morning, with crowds easing after midday. A later arrival means more breathing room and a more relaxed browse.

🚶 Walk, ride or take public transport if you are able to. It is a beautiful 30 minute stroll along the river from the Canning Bridge train station and one of our favourite ways to arrive on a Sunday morning.

This year, NEO Gallery presents a programme that brings Indonesian modern and contemporary art together, with an emphasis on creating dialogue across generations and artistic approaches. By placing works from different periods alongside one another, the gallery hopes to show the connections between them and how artistic ideas and visual languages evolve over time.

Rather than concentrating on a single theme or medium, NEO Gallery is interested in how artists from different periods respond to the world around them, and how their practices reflect the social, cultural, and personal contexts of their time.

The gallery’s programme brings together artists whose practices engage with personal, social, and cultural experiences in distinct ways; particularly drawn to works that allow for multiple readings, where a specific story or context can open up broader conversations around identity, memory, place, nature, and everyday life. By placing different generations and perspectives in conversation, NEO gallery aims to highlight both the continuities and changes within Indonesian art while giving each artist’s practice the context and space it deserves.

Orquestra Pacifico Tropical on the Pickathon Cherry Hill Stage

Over the last couple years, two of the major highlights at @pickathon have been local artists and Cumbia acts. @o_p_t_ checks both boxes. Co-founded by David “Papi” Fimbres, who performed at the festival with Reyna Tropical last year, Orquestra Pacifico Tropical was born in Portland in 2012 with a mission to bring Cumbia to the city. More than a dozen years later, the local favorites continue to win people over with their infectious live shows. 

OPT was recommended to me specifically by a friend who knew we'd be at Pickathon and had recently seen them do a free show in town. A Portland resident for longer than the group's existence, he'd only just discovered them himself and was blown away. 

Living in Seattle, that concept of being blind to so much of what's happening in my own city is easy to identify with. Having local acts like this booked at the festival doesn't only benefit those of us visiting from outside of the area, but it shines a light on the talent that passes by those living among them, even those firmly entrenched in the music scene. Acts like Forty Feet Tall, Rhododendron, Buddy Wynkoop, Cosmic Tones Research Trio, and, of course, OPT, have earned so many fans locally, as well as visiting from afar, just based on incredibly strong appearances at Pickathon.

As for the increased representation of Cumbia on Pendarvis Farm, it's been enthusiastically embraced by attendees. OPT plays a major role in continuing to grow that appreciation by creating an experience where the music seeps into the audience, so we can feel it. Once it's in your blood, we're discussing something beyond sound or rhythms. It takes over like the holy ghost. You're in it. An OPT concert is elevated to an instant party and communal experience. In other words, a perfect booking to match the Pickathon ethos.
.
.
#orquestrapacificotropical #pickathon #cumbia.

Shadows of Time by Peter Neilson @peterneilsonsculpture

The future, the past and the space in between. Peter's latest sculpture embodies the ongoing movement and transition of shadows from past objects to the present. Fabricated from pieces of corten steel left over from his plasma cut art forms of Australian native animals, plants and flowers with each part carefully hand forged and artfully placed together until a new world emerged. Seemingly held together by the mutual attraction of space and shadows. We exist in time, but can we exist without shadows!

Portal for the Soul, a mirror sphere, the soul, swings gently through a coffin-shaped doorway, marking the 
passage between life and death. The polished surface reflects all who stand before it, inviting them to see 
themselves within this liminal space. The doorway is both an ending and a beginning, a threshold we all 
must cross, where the self is carried forward beyond the frame of the body. Imagining the possibility of 
communication, like signals carried on an aerial reaching beyond the threshold.

Metropolyps by Suzy Syme & Andrew Costa @thetidepooldesigns

In an era where ecological systems and constructed environments are increasingly intertwined, Metropolyps 
blurs the boundary between sculpture and inhabitable form. Inspired by brain coral, the foundational 
structure of reef ecosystems, the work draws on the logic of collective growth. Fabricated from plant-based 
biopolymer, the installation is composed of uniquely formed, interdependent elements ranging from small, 
intimate forms to human-scale structures. By inviting close bodily proximity, Metropolyps reflects the reef’s 
spatial complexity, adaptability, and living architecture.

Melting Man by Ajay Thomas @recalibrate.public

Melting Man is a hydromechanical sculpture that transforms using the simple logic of a child's push puppet. He is held upright by a system of internal cords kept in tension by a counterweight. When tension is maintained, the statue stands ridged. Instead of a child's thumb triggering a collapsure, Melting Man's transformation occurs through tidal fluctuations. A ballast sits within the sculpture's base, at low tide, the ballast hangs and its weight maintains tension in the cords, keeping the him ridged. When the tide rises, the ballast is engulfed by water, losing its wight and slackening the cords, which causes him to collapse under his own weight.

Mo' Money is a lawn mower dressed up as royalty. Finished in fake gold and crowned at its motorhead, it transforms a suburban workhorse into a monument to status, aspiration and the Australian dream. Mo' Money pokes fun at Australia's national obsession with home ownership, the preoccupation with property prices and the belief that a patch of grass is a measure of success. proposing this sculpture as a station for global peace and manifestation. Dedicated to anti-war, anti-poverty, and anti-discrimination values, the work broadcasts a synchronised message of love to the furthest corners of the earth, promoting a world where diversity is celebrated as a beautiful mosaic.

We started planning the second life for all of the donated wood for Pickathon a year ago. Matchmaking architects with builders and nonprofits to ensure the wood did not go to waste and that it would be utilized for hands-on trade education. 2026 is our most successful year to date. The proof is in the list below. These organizations received materials from each of the neighborhoods and stages at Pickathon.

Parrot Creek, Girls that Build, Sabin-Schellenberg Technical Professional Center, PSU Iteck Center, P:ear Mentor, Oasis Day Center, Dream Big City, Sabin CDC, PSU Oak Savanna, Blackbird Public Arts, Q-Side Skatepark, Menucha Retreat and Conference Center, Cedarwood Waldorf School, and the Waterside Renewal Foundation.

For all the folks that didn't quite understand why we started the nonprofit, I hope this helps and excites you about helping out in the future. There were a lot of doors shut in our face this year. We applied for and were denied an OCF grant to develop an Afro Futurist Neighborhood at Pickathon 2027. It would have featured African American vendors, architects, sound engineers, performers, and students learning new skills. We also applied for a Nike grant to start a summer dance program in partnership with Bodyvox for underserved kids that would have culminated in a performance at Pickathon 2027. Sadly, we didn't get funding, but our hopes are high in seeing these plans come to fruition in the future with the help of our community.

Looking forward to getting started on partnerships and programs for 2027.

See you on the farm.

Matt Wagner 
Executive director

Guy Humphries, a prodigious metal artist, masterfully transforms recycled materials into captivating art. His 
Driftwoody sculpture is a whimsical cartoon depicting two eager surfers whose Woody van is comically bogged in sand, nose-first into a palm tree. They desperately dig it out, capturing the hilarious mayhem of beach days. Guy's genius lies in conjuring magnificence from the mundane, meticulously salvaging discarded remnants from skip bins, sheds, backyards and dumps across Queensland. He's a true champion of sustainable artistry, turning refuse into profound beauty and shared delight.

The Blue Channeled Channel Beacon by @christophertrotter

A misguided guiding Beacon
Channel Markers, Buoys and Beacons are dynamic eye catching structures about our waterways.
What they actually mean remains a mystery to so many, yet their meanings are so important to those that are 
guided by them.
Inspired by memories of motoring about the Gold Coast waterways in a tinny, here discarded outboard motor 
legs have been given a new life in the form of an inverted triangle channel marker.
However, in this case, it's purpose will always remain a mystery.

The Invited Artist of SWELL Sculpture Festival 2026 | @patricia.piccinini 🦌🍄‍🟫🏍️

Salute to the Sun continues the artist's long fascination with the boundary we draw between the natural and the artificial — and how readily that line dissolves once you look closely. This new bronze sculpture is a chimera, seamlessly moving between deer, tree, fungus, human and motorcycle. It evolves out of a machine base into an organic form whose arms, or perhaps antlers, unfurl like budding leaves.

Patricia's art has exhibited and is held in collections wordwide - her practice examines the increasingly nebulous boundary between the artificial and the natural as it appears in contemporary culture and ideas. Her surreal drawings, hybrid animals and vehicular creatures question the way that contemporary technology and culture changes our understanding of what it means to be human and wonders at our relationships with – and responsibilities towards – that which we create. While ethics are central, her approach is ambiguous and questioning rather than moralistic and didactic.

“A lot of the topics that I’m writing about are heavy, and I feel like it was hard for me, growing up in modern music, to find something that touched on deep topics and wasn’t just sad music,” Pomeroy says. She pauses, then starts to laugh, softly and darkly, adding, “But I do write for the disturbed.”

This excerpt is taken from a press release for Oklahoma singer-songwriter, @kenpomeroymusic. The 22-year-old Cherokee musician is currently hitting the European festival circuit followed by Nashville and Durham dates, before a string of slots opening for artists like Iron & Wine, Old Crowe Medicine Show, and Jim James through December.

We liked the songs we'd heard before her Cherry Hill set on the first night of @pickathon, but Pomeroy's live show is on another level. Despite her claims of suffering from "RBF," Ken's personality is hard not to love. Her dry wit was on full display, contrasting between the beautiful, affecting nature and sincerity of the music it bumpered. There's a perfect balance of youthful radiance in what reads as an almost otherworldly and deeply seasoned wisdom in her work. There's a raw honesty to it all. She knows how to mine the core.

Her bassist had recently been fired, but we didn't notice anything lacking. The warm, comfort of Pomeroy's music feels like a sunset. I look forward to it carrying us through the colder months. In certain areas, the song in this clip is even reminiscent of Nick Drake.

Pomeroy playfully jabbed at her bandmates and I noticed a surprising amount of lyrics and references to dogs throughout her set. More importantly, she took a moment to speak on mental health, stating that she recently began taking medication to treat her own. Ken Pomeroy is a perfect example of a younger generation of artists from historically conservative areas like the Bible belt who stand on a tradition of beautiful textures and heartfelt lyricism, while outright rejecting ignorant and oppressive rhetoric and stereotypes often associated with those regions. Acknowledging social injustices and stigmas, while expressing a desire for a more equitable world doesn't undermine the music. It reflects strength and makes it more powerful

#Installation "Improvisations in the Park", de @larrybellstudio está presentando en @madsqparknyc su mayor instalación pública hasta la fecha y la primera al aire libre en Nueva York. En estas últimas semanas, la instalación ha adquirido una nueva dimensión tras la llegada del invierno a la ciudad. La exposición reúne seis esculturas monumentales de vidrio que refractan, absorben y transmiten la luz, dialogando con los árboles, las sombras y el perfil urbano que rodea el parque. Lejos de ser objetos estáticos, las piezas se transforman continuamente, revelando cómo el tiempo, el clima y la percepción convierten la experiencia escultórica en algo vivo. ⁠

#Installation "Disruption as Rapture" es una instalación pública al aire libre de @shahzia.sikander, presentada en el @nasjonalmuseet y visible hasta el marzo de 2026. ⁠
⁠
Sikander trabaja a partir de un manuscrito del siglo XVIII y de la tradición de la miniatura del sur y centro de Asia, que reimagina como “dibujos cinéticos”: ilustraciones hechas a mano y animadas digitalmente. Al igual que la propia tradición miniaturista —que viajó de las cortes persas a los talleres otomanos y los manuscritos mogoles—, la obra reflexiona sobre el desplazamiento de imágenes, técnicas y lenguajes a través del tiempo y las culturas.⁠
⁠

INNER CIRCLE invites visitors to contemplate reflection and connection. The work is formed from translucent discs that frame shifting views both inward and outward, the work explores the relationship between personal responsibility and collective action. Looking inwards, we are encouraged to consider our values, choices and capacity for change. Looking outwards, we are reminded that our actions ripple through families, communities and society. The circular form symbolises unity, equality and shared purpose. Viewer’s become part of the artwork itself, reflecting on how a better world begins within each of us and grows through all of us together.

Tomorrow, Hypertemples wakes up.

Right now, the work is sitting inside @hotagc in its dormant state, an exhibition waiting for humans to activate it.

For thousands of years, cultures around the world have activated sacred sites, objects, bodies, architecture and places through ritual: through protocols, offerings, movement, sound, gesture, intention and rites of passage.

Tomorrow, we do exactly that.

I’m inviting you to become part of a very special collective spell for liberation “Opening Ceremony” of Hyper Temples at @bleachfestival 

This is not about being a professional performer.
You don’t need to be an artist.
You don’t need experience.

This is an ageless, genderless, all-inclusive space for anyone curious enough to enter, explore, play, get radical and become part of something completely unique.

From 10AM, we’ll gather, warm up, meet one another and begin sharing the stories we bring into the space.

Together we’ll explore the UnitePlayPerform methodology and co-design a series of simple, beautiful gestures using movement, words, sound and ritual.

We’ll work with masks, costumes, bodysuits, adornments, flags, banners, crystals, sculptural objects and sound tools.

By 12PM, we’ll have mapped the HOTA exhibition and surrounding spaces and created the collective score.

Then from 1–2PM, Hypertemples comes alive.

We’ll perform the work together, activate the exhibition and invite the public into the spell.

You’ll leave having experienced some of the practices, processes and tools behind how we Unite. Play. Perform.

If you want to be inside the deeper co-design, ritual and activation, apply through the link *places are limited.

If you simply want to witness or join us as part of the public activation, come to HOTA at 1PM sharp tomorrow.

Come help us wake the temples.

Become part of the collective spell.

#Exhibition "A Letter Lost in the Offline Refuge" es la primera exposición individual de @gripface_ en @yiri.arts. Concebida como una instalación inmersiva y site-specific, la muestra articula pintura e instalación como un único cuerpo narrativo. En el centro del espacio, una gran cabina espejada actúa como núcleo físico y conceptual, generando un juego constante entre el reflejo del visitante, la arquitectura y las obras pictóricas que orbitan alrededor.⁠
⁠
El proyecto nace de un relato escrito por el propio artista durante una estancia en los Dolomitas italianos: la historia de una tribu que, ante el colapso ecológico y económico del mundo contemporáneo, decide retirarse y construir una forma de vida autosuficiente, un “refugio offline”. La exposición traslada esa ficción al espacio expositivo, proponiendo un escenario donde imagen, cuerpo y relato ensayan otras posibilidades de coexistencia.⁠
⁠

Mary Halvorson took the Cherry Hill stage at @pickathon in flats and a breezy summer outfit that looked more like she was coming from a nice lunch date than about to tear open new sonic landscapes with her jazz quartet. The Massachusetts native arranged her music stand, rummaged through the handbag she'd placed at her side, and adjusted her spectacles, before casually sending lightning quick flurries down her guitar neck and exhibiting why she's remained such a universally lauded player for the better part of two decades. 

I have such tremendous respect for her that I don't want my descriptions to be misinterpreted, but Halvorson visually presents a Shelly Long energy, if she had Freaky Friday swapped with Mahavishnu: John McLaughlin. Everything about her is powerful, yet understated. Stoic and composed, her dextrous finger-work looks as effortless as breathing. The papers on her stand could just as easily be a shopping list. All of the emotion comes out in the music.

Appearance isn't important, other than to highlight how the decorated guitarist defies outdated expectations or categorization in her work. This is especially relevant in an environment like Pickathon that isn't overly jazz-centric, but always intentional about injecting that component into the programming. A petite, 5-foot white woman likely clashes with the one-dimensional stereotype many outside the genre have about what a jazz musician "looks like." At Pickathon, people who may otherwise never attend a jazz show witnessed Mary demonstrate how skill and vision is king and, if you possess them, others will follow you anywhere. Last year, the brilliant bassist, Anna Butterss taught a similar lesson. As a parent who loves Pickathon, I can't help but consider how these magnificent performances are being absorbed by and inspiring the next generation.

I first became aware of the Portland project, @buddywynkoop through artist Joshua McQuary (@mc__monster) who was traveling with them and "peddling his wares" as he put it. I've posted McMonster's work both on this account and my website and we DM each other occasionally - sometimes about our hatred of AI - but I never met him in person, so I was disappointed to have a conflicting engagement when they came through Seattle in October. When Buddy Wynkoop's name appeared on this year's @Pickathon lineup, I figured it was time to finally see what McQuary has been hyping up.

I gave them a quick listen last year and vaguely remembered thinking they were some form of post-punk or garage rock outfit. Something with a little energy. The song on the Pickathon Playlist was a frenetic number that reminded me of festival veterans, Parquet Courts in the most positive way. I liked it, but I needed to see more.

We pulled it together in time to get to the Grove stage at noon on Saturday. Since its introduction, the Grove has been known to host wild daytime sets by acts like Wine Lips, Gel, and Frankie & The Witch Fingers. I was expecting something high energy and fun, but I didn't know if it would go beyond that. There's a benefit to being lumped into something like a post-punk or psych revival scene/movement, but the challenge is to separate oneself from the pack. For example, when everyone is swallowing the mic and letting out the trademark "woooh," there's a risk of hitting the ceiling as a John Dwyer clone. The good ones carve identities of their own.

Despite any references or potential influences, Wynkoop doesn't suffer from being one-dimensional. The art punk group has a touch of that Courts vibe mixed in with a dose of Viagra Boys, the way a lurching, staggered delivery can suddenly lock into a propulsive glide through a roller coaster track. There's an Idles-like directness and inevitable DEVO comparison in the shout sung vocals and angular rhythms, but collectively, they just sound like Buddy Wynkoop. They broke all misconceptions. It turns out they're actually pretty great.

This year's @pickathon was overloaded with so much talent that it made whittling out a definitive gameplan next to impossible. If something jumped out at me from the festival playlist, I'd try to mentally log the artists names and reference that cerebral rolodex on the fly as we navigated the schedule throughout the weekend.

Prewn played the first of two sets on Saturday afternoon on the Grove stage. A project of North Hampton, Massachusetts songwriter, Izzy Hagerup, the most that my dehydrated mind could recall was that they had something worth checking out. If it didn't blow us away, we would relax backstage, eat ice cream, and charge our power banks while they played in the background. 

I was in Goldilocks mode and not everything is gonna hit in this setting. Timing and stage can be major factors in how successful an artist might connect. A 2pm performance at the Grove is a tricky slot, especially 3 days in. The rowdier garage psych acts tend to do well, because it's hard to ignore them. The more serene artists work if it's a mood you're looking for. Several hammocks are strung up between trees at the back of the crowd for those looking to really zone out.

Prewn isn't going to crack you over the head with waves of fuzz guitar and blistering solos or lull you into a meditative state with gentle melodies. They bring something that is somehow neither, yet in-between. The moment we approached I knew I wasn't going anywhere. I was locked in. 

How do you draw someone in and hold their attention while their brains are dying? Prewn's approach is to go straight for the gut. There is something raw and authentic about these songs that injects itself into the bloodstream. There's a subtle aggression to the music; grime and rust, vintage brass and patina. It's unassuming, but dynamic. Hagerup's voice has a timeless quality that cuts through everything, as the tunes rise and crash like driftwood bodies on jagged rocks. They stumble through bramble and collapse into lavender with bleeding shins. It's as if they are discovering their power in real time.

If this video does anything for you, consider investigating further. It's worth it.

The Listening Sea presents abstract two forms inspired by the shape of a whale’s cochlea. Constructed from ceramic elements and PET plastic, the work responds to wind and proximity. As air passes through, small bells ring and recycled plastic softly resonates, creating a gentle auditory experience. Rather than focusing on damage, the sculpture invites mindful listening and celebrates the increasing guardianship of marine health. It acknowledges positive action, collective responsibility, and the progress being made towards ocean conservation and climate awareness, inviting coastal visitors to participate in this evolving story.

San Francisco's Acid King (@acidkingrocks) were at the forefront of the stoner rock and psychedelic doom metal movements coming out of California in the early 90s. 33 years later, they continue to hypnotize crowds by unfurling thick suffocating blankets of hazy distorted sound. 

The Bay Area trio played the @pickathon Woods Stage on Friday, July 31st, delivering a set that we'd continue to hear about throughout the weekend. I was reluctantly convinced to miss it in favor of something else, but from what we heard, it was all-out pandemonium that resulted in security being brought in to contain it.

The next day, we managed to catch a brief recording session with the band at the unadvertised SLAB stage, where I managed to get a portrait of them posing in front of a sick-ass painting of skeleton horses and flames. 

With her small stature, frontwoman Lori S. can be a somewhat unassuming figure, until she picks up her guitar and sends her reverb-drenched vocals rippling into the Stratosphere. The members are incredibly approachable despite the brutality of their riffs. One moment they're opening a hell mouth, unleashing all manner of demonic spectres from the netherworld, and the next, they're thanking everyone for showing up and handing out guitar pics, or affably waving from the gator as they roll by.

This clip was shot at a 1pm Sunday set in the Galaxy barn.The moshpit didn't get out of hand or plunge the room into bedlam as it had in the Woods, but the doom still rose from the Earth like magma; a sonic behemoth striking us square in the chest. The toned down afternoon lessened the risk of my camera getting smashed into pieces.

ACID KING was another great booking adding dimension to Pickathon's lineup and I love it when we see artists enjoying the property throughout the festival. Later that afternoon, we found the imposing leather vest-clad body of bassist, Bryce Shelton gently swaying in a hammock. They belong here.

Another great Pickathon, including a mid-act wedding…a Pickathon first!

It's hard to believe that the first day of @pickathon 2026 was already a week ago and we're still recovering. Even more difficult is describing the experience of attending the festival. 

Not only do things shift from year to year, but from artist to artist, day to night, and "neighborhood" to neighborhood. There is so much depth and variety at the Happy Valley, Oregon festival. I ran into a friend yesterday who told me it was impossible to describe what it's like without going there. That may be true, but that doesn't mean it isn't my job to attempt it.

Each of the different stage areas are constructed to have their own energy and personalities and within those spaces it can drastically change from one act to the next. On Day 1, we caught a wild, frenetic set from @meatbodiesofficialauthentic; a lighthearted, yet beautiful and affecting performance from @kenpomeroymusic; and enjoyed an infectious cumbia dance party with @o_p_t_ all on the Cherry Hill stage alone.

Pickathon is intended to be immersive with it's meticulously crafted, hand-made wooden structures designed to illuminate and come to life as the sun goes down and the art seamlessly embedded into the forest landscape.

I use my words to the best of my ability, but we also shot thousands of digital images, multiple rolls of analog film (currently being processed), a dozen or so videos, and handfuls of cell phone images as visual aids to bridge those gaps when descriptors fall short.

Here is a selection of phone pics taken on DAY 1. The initial plan was to post these on-site at the end of each day, but plans can erode and morph when you're immersed in that world. In the aftermath, these operate more as a breadcrumb trail; little vignettes with the purpose of cobbling a more cohesive understanding of the world we meld into and give ourselves over to year after year. 2026 was another one for the books. Hopefully, even a glimpse of that magic is reflected.

More to come....

May all of our interactions and imprints be deep and positive on all and everything.

By the final day, our aging bodies were spent.

Nighttime in the woods is magical, but there's a different appeal to the stage in the daytime, where sunlight speckles and shines through the majestic arboreal canopy and the planet feels as if it is waking up with you. After going hard on night one, we made sure to start our Friday at 11am seated at the Woods Stage for a rejuvenating performance by @thecosmictonesresearchtrio. Next month, @marcosvalle_oficial will turn 83 years old, but, more than 6 decades after releasing his debut album, the Brazilian music legend shows no signs of slowing down. Seeing his inclusion at this year's @pickathon was the biggest draw for me during the initial lineup announcement. Although Marcos only did one set during the festival, he more than lived up to the hype. I feel lucky to have finally been able to catch him. Seeing him in a space as important to us as Pendarvis Farm only made it that much more special.

Valle's performance fell on Saturday, melding perfectly into the landscape and beautiful summer evening. Tunes like "Samba de Verão" aka "Summer Samba" were like a cool refreshing waterfall at that point in the hot dusty weekend. This song, in particular, set off little alerts of recognition for many who, otherwise, couldn't place Valle by name and were unsure if they'd know any of his compositions. 

A familiarity with his career or accolades isn't a prerequisite to enjoy a show by the man who helped popularize Bossa Nova to the world. That said, I was pleasantly surprised to see young fans who I wouldn't necessarily expect to know his work be as versed on his catalog and excited by his appearance as anyone. 

The legacy of Marcos Valle continues to reverberate, bringing together fans from all ages. He offers nostalgia for some and inspiration for others, but everyone gets transported to a cool, infectious world of soulful grooves, latin jazz and samba.

Forging the Coast by Neumann Group @neumannsteelaustralia

Forging the Coast is a four-arc portal structure that symbolises the combined strength and contribution of the Neumann Group companies in shaping the Gold Coast since 1948. 
Each arc represents a key part of the group’s operations and materials: 
Reinforcing steel arc – Neumann Steel 
Mineral sand arc – Currumbin Minerals 
Fabricated steel arc – Neumann Contractors 
Plastic arc – Neumann Injection Moulding 
The material palette combines reinforcing steel, fabricated structural steel, mineral aggregates, and recycled plastic, reflecting the real materials used daily across Neumann Group operations.

Marina Perez Simão features in "Recipes for Broken Hearts", the first Bukhara Biennial @bukhara.biennial in Uzbekistan.⁠
⁠
Marina Perez Simão marinasimao__, in collaboration with Bakhtiyar Babamuradov (Uzbekistan), created Untitled (2025), a huge mosaic on the floor of a historic caravanserai in the region. Using colorful ceramic pieces produced in Uzbekistan to compose a 105 x 160 meter figure, the installation goes beyond the boundaries of abstraction and transcends the tangible through colors and shapes that suggest movement.⁠
⁠
Curated by Diana Campbell, Recipes for Broken Hearts brings together global and regional artists alongside Uzbekistan’s master artisans. Remarkably, every work was produced here, in Uzbekistan – a tribute to the enduring power of local craft and collaboration.⁠
⁠
From Sep 9 to Nov 23, 2025⁠
Bukhara Biennial | Ayozzhon Karvonsaroyi, Historic Center of Bukhara, Bukhara, Uzbekistan⁠
⁠
📷 Photo by Felix Odell, Images courtesy of Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation⁠

Jennifer Latour @bonjourlatour crea flores que no existen en la naturaleza. Corta y conecta diferentes plantas para dar forma a nuevas especies imaginarias. Cada escultura está hecha a mano, con la precisión de alguien formado en maquillaje de efectos especiales.⁠
⁠
En lugar de ocultar los cortes, los muestra. Las uniones entre tallos y pétalos forman parte de la obra. Construir algo extraño y bello a partir de lo que ya existe. El resultado te lleva a un estado tanto natural como irreal. ⁠
⁠
Su trabajo es más bien un experimento silencioso: ¿Y si las plantas pudieran prestarse partes entre sí? ¿Y si la evolución fuera rápida, caótica y se llevara a cabo en el salón de alguien?⁠
⁠

The frog has always been a symbol of a healthy ecosystem—a reminder that when the environment thrives, so does everything around it. This year, it became a symbol of the people who make Pickathon what it is.

The stages are coming down, the dust is settling, and Pendarvis Farm is slowly returning to its everyday rhythm. Every year we’re reminded just how difficult it is to say goodbye to this place.

Thank you to every artist, maker, volunteer, crew member, partner, vendor, neighbor, and every person who joined us on the farm. Your generosity, curiosity, creativity, and care are what transform these woods into something extraordinary.

Pickathon is a place of discovery. A world unto itself. For a few days Pendarvis Farm becomes home to unexpected moments, lifelong friendships, unforgettable performances, and the kind of magic that can only be experienced, never fully explained.

We say it every year because somehow it’s always true: this was our best year yet.

Thank you for believing in what we build together. We’ll see you back on the farm next summer. 💚🐸

#Installation For @aichi_triennale 2025, Minerva Cuevas presents a large-scale relief mural (11 m x 4 m) installed at the entrance hall of the Seto City Art Museum, a key hub for culture and the arts in Seto, Japan.⁠
⁠
The mural features motifs inspired by Kitagawa Tamiji (1894-1989), a painter who was deeply influenced by Mexican muralism and the model of open-air art schools he learned about and directed during his time in Mexico (1921-1936). It also features symbolic elements, including animals, video game characters, and corporate logos. The artwork highlights Kitagawaʼs cultural significance in Seto and his focus on art education and his care for children, as well as elements that evoke both pre-Columbian and contemporary Japanese cultures.⁠
⁠
Cuevasʼs mural not only honors the artistic histories of both countries but also invites reflection on the relationship between art, community, and social responsibility. It rises like a contemporary ruin where past and present converge.⁠
⁠
⁠

#Installation El artista @franco_mazzucchelli es uno de los pioneros en realizar instalaciones hinchables y en desafiar a los materiales al uso que se utilizaban al aire libre con otros menos convencionales.⁠
⁠
Formado en la multiforme área de lo conceptual de los años 60, su producción artística se ha caracterizado desde el principio por el empleo de materiales sintéticos de producción industrial legados a la contemporaneidad y de tradición relativamente reciente, cuyo conocimiento es como objetos de empleo común.⁠
⁠
Los materiales han sido para Mazzucchelli objeto de búsqueda y experimentación con los que ha contribuido a extender la revolución formal de las primeras vanguardias a ámbitos estéticos y sociales más extensos.⁠
⁠
Imágenes: Franco Muzzecchelli⁠

Migrating by Mang Hong Vincent Lee @vinex.art

This sculpture depicts a group of Eastern Curlews, the world’s largest migratory shorebirds, on their global 
journey. Found in regions ranging from Australia to Northern habitats, these birds represent a tireless struggle for survival. Through this work, the artist captures their inherent beauty while reminding us of the magnificent life sharing our planet. The choice of rusty metal sheets for the welded sculpture serves as a narrative device; the weathered texture symbolises the passage of time and the physical toll of ageing that the animals endure throughout their long migration.

Takeaway Tides by Lauren Gray @pieces_of_ginger

Takeaway Tides transforms the humble soy sauce fish into a glowing school that hovers between memory and 
environment. Referencing takeaway meals, shared rituals, and mass production, the work explores how familiar objects become vessels for collective experience. Arranged as a drifting shoal, the forms echo tidal movement and communal behaviour. As night falls, the sculpture gently illuminates, shifting from playful nostalgia to reflective pause, inviting viewers to consider the relationship between consumption, habit, and the coastal landscapes we occupy and depend upon.

Totem Crush by Elizabeth O'Connor @elizabeth_oconnor

Beyond holding colour, form and texture in delicate harmony, these crushed metal totems explore the poetic 
interplay between resilience and vulnerability. Shaped by the artist's hands and body through a process of 
controlled distortion, the folds and furrows within their contoured surfaces echo the fragility of lived experience. As light shifts, the sculptures cast elongated shadows that become extensions of the work itself. Viewed from multiple angles, their forms continually transform, inviting the viewer to slow down, move around them and discover moments of stillness within an ever-changing sculptural equilibrium.

I Once Was A Mountain by Michelle Walker @michellewalkerart

Michelle Walker’s linear sculpture of reclaimed brick and scrap metal has the phrase ‘I Once Was A Mountain’ painted across the brick faces. A quiet declaration spoken by the land itself. The line mimics Wollumbin’s 
profile, a geological feature that formed the Gold Coast hinterland ranges. Through repurposing, the work draws
attention to the link between object, raw material and source landscape. Mountains erode to soil; soil into brick; brick crumbles to rubble. Within Michelle’s art practice, rubble is not an end point - it becomes pigment, paint and new expression.

Light Along the Littoral by Jo Norton @thrownbyjo

Light Along the Littoral is an installation of handbuilt ceramic solar lights marking the littoral zone where land 
and sea meet. Mounted on tall metal poles and solar-powered, the lights respond to the rhythms of the 
shoreline, where light, movement, and change are constant. Each hand-shaped vessel references shells, eroded stone, and tidal markings. The Weight of Becoming by David O'Brien @davidobriens_art

Weight of Becoming explores the tension between intent, artistic expression, play, and discovery through the manipulation of material in space. Influenced by architectural form, structure, and the relationship between built and natural environments, the paired sculptures reflect an accumulation of ideas, experiences, and aspirations formed through years of balancing professional and creative life. Emerging through experimentation and persistence, they embody creative growth and artistic identity. Like guardian lions marking an entrance, these forms stand as symbols of arrival and presence. Through Corten steel and concrete, they express weathering, transformation, and permanence, carrying forward a lasting legacy of creative becoming.

I had a great time presenting this week at a Sustainable Building Week event hosted by the Portland Materials Transparency Collaborative. I chatted about how Creative Neighborhoods gives a second life to materials used at Pickathon by partnering with other nonprofits in need.

This year, before the festival, I worked with Parrot Creek Family Services and Holst Architecture to design outdoor structures that would be used in the Lucky neighborhood during Pickathon to provide shade and seating for festivalgoers. After the festival, the structures went to Parrot Creek to become a series of shelters along a trail for clients to use.

It was also great to see presentations from PSU architecture students who contributed to the last two Cherry Hill stages. Did you know that the recycled fishing nets used as the backdrop for this year's Cherry Hill stage went to Ukraine after the festival to help defend against drone attacks?

I am really looking forward to all the amazing things we have planned for the coming year with Pickathon 2027 and other partners.

Trades - Education - Art

Thanks to the PMTC and Brightworks for hosting.

Urban Chorus by Monte Lupo Collaborators @montelupoarts

This sculpture shows people mid‑conversation as parrots perch among them, mirroring their gestures and rhythms as if speaking in another language. The birds act as participants rather than observers, dissolving the line between humans and native fauna. Loud and social, parrots reflect the energy of Australian urban life. The work invites us to consider who is heard, who repeats, who interrupts and who belongs. It explores how we share space and listen within overlapping voices. The parrots animate the scene, creating a living chorus of movement and sound.

Family by Jennifer Rowe @jenn.kooroo.rowe

Family sculptured from Huon Pine (Tasmanian), brings together two entwined histories of violence and survival.
The chained thylacines (Tasmania tiger) reference the Tasmanian Black War, when First Nations people were 
rounded up, shackled, and forcibly removed from their country. The thylacine, perceived farming threat, was 
hunted to extinction. The chains bind animal and human histories, exposing how colonial systems justified 
dispossession and massacre. While the thylacine was silenced forever, First Nations people endured. This work insists on remembrance, acknowledgement and the truth that survival itself is an act of resistance.

@thee.quasi made their long overdue @pickathon debut with a set in the Galaxy Barn on Saturday night. The organ and drums duo are local Portland legends, born from the ashes of the project Motorgoat in 1993. They're a band that I feel has never really gotten the attention that they deserve. A lot of people know the name, but not enough of them know the work. 

Sam Coomes would join his friend Elliott Smith in Heatmiser in 1994 for the band's final album and tour. Quasi would later operate as Smith's backing band for a tour when the late artist emerged with his short-lived but brilliant solo career. With Janet Weiss becoming the long-term drummer for Sleater-Kinney, their associations to other high-profile projects has sometimes drawn focus over their work together. As a longtime fan whose been seeing them for decades, there's nothing better than what the pair churn out as a unit between them. They whip up sonic maelstroms that swell and crash, reform and explode. It's majestic and ragged. Quasi are the musical equivalent of creating a tornado in a bottle.

From Billy Strings to Geese, Pickathon has become known for platforming young artists who go on to break out on massive scales, but what really shone this year is the effect of bringing in seasoned veterans and presenting them to a new audience. One of my favorite things I heard this year is that people were discussing the Quasi barn set, asking one another if they caught it and expressing how revelatory and explosive it was for them. I missed the band's later set in the Woods, but I have no doubt that it just as amazing. 

For everyone who just discovered this beautifully dynamic, and chaotic world of pummeling drums, sweet harmonies, and unrestrainable skronking, welcome. Glad you made it.

The barn was packed, but I managed to squeeze into the side stage area until I popped out and spilled on the back corner of the stage itself. The angle I recorded this from isn't necessarily ideal, but hopefully it provides a glimpse into what they do/did. I couldn't see much of Janet's face throughout the show, but it's a testament to her abilities that she remains such a powerful, radiating force regardless.

But there's more than just okonomiyaki! 😋

🍳 Osaka-Style Okonomiyaki: their signature dish, made from a treasured family recipe
🍖 Chashu Rice Bowl: tender, flavourful chashu served over warm rice
🍙 Onigiri: classic Japanese rice balls, perfect for a quick bite between stalls

Whether you're already an okonomiyaki fan or trying it for the very first time, this is your chance to experience the flavours of Osaka right here in Perth. Authentic flavours, family tradition and Japanese comfort food made with care 🥰

🎙️ Sexta é sinónimo de novo episódio do podcast Portugal Manual.

Chegámos ao último episódio desta temporada, gravada ao vivo no @bicadosapato durante a Lisbon Design Week, onde, ao longo de 11 episódios, reunimos algumas das vozes que estão hoje a pensar, criar e transformar o design contemporâneo.

E fechamos esta temporada com Michele Fajtmann fundadora da Lisbon Design Week, e @joanaastolfi designer, arquiteta e artista.

Uma conversa que parte desta última edição da Lisbon Design Week para pensar o crescimento do festival, a sua relação cada vez mais próxima com a arte e o papel que pode ter na afirmação do design português dentro e fora do país.

Falamos também da estreia do Lisbon Design Week Lounge na ARCO Lisboa pensado por Joana Astolfi como uma verdadeira sala de estar no centro da feira, reunindo mais de uma centena de peças e criando um espaço de encontro, pausa e descoberta.

Que lugar ocupa hoje o design português no contexto internacional? Como pode a colaboração entre designers, artesãos e marcas fortalecer este ecossistema? E como pode um evento independente continuar a crescer sem perder a sua identidade?

Uma conversa sobre design, cidade, colaboração e sobre o caminho que ainda temos pela frente.

Com este episódio fechamos uma temporada de 11 conversas que ficam disponíveis para ouvir no Spotify e Apple Podcasts. Se ainda não ouviram todas, aproveitem a pausa de verão para descobrir, ou revisitar, os convidados, projetos e ideias que passaram por aqui.

Em setembro voltamos. E voltamos com muitas novidades. 👀

🎨We're back for our Sweet 16th!  Graffiato returns over Labour Weekend with a whole new slate of incredible artists and walls to paint. 

📢There are a few special mentions for this year. 
- 2x international artists (literally flying over for Graffiato...how cool!)
- 2x new emerging local artists (from volunteer to x-mas tree painter to a Graffiato wall...it's what dreams are made of)
- We'll all be in the same laneway!  This is the best part for the organisers 😅

Artist announcements and map of locations to come...We can't wait to bring big colour back to the streets of Taupō!

We wanted to hear from the team of @kell.sunshine & @rebeccaterborg_illustration to find out how they approached and enjoyed their collab together.  The results speak for themselves, of course, but you can't get this level of insight anywhere else.

From Kell Sunshine:
How did you approach this collab?
"Our collab started with a berry, a suggestion of colour, and we bounced emails back and forward til there was a finished design. It was a delight sending my contributions away and receiving a developed surprise via email a few days later.

I felt that designing as a collab took some of the [self- imposed) pressure off, allowing me to approach the design lightly and more freely."

What did you feel you achieved during the process?
"On the wall, Rebecca and Nigel and I were able to talk shop all day and casually float a tonne of random questions at each other about process. I particularly loved being nudged to approach lines and shapes in new ways, shifting out of my entrenched methodologies. 

The collab process feels beautiful because it takes us out of our well-trodden path as artists, creating space for new approaches and nuances."

Great work ladies!  And a special shoutout to @dagarmedia for the huge mahi over Graffiato weekend.

@sean_duffell, you knocked it out of the park with this pairing!

🎙️ Sexta é sinónimo de novo episódio do podcast Portugal Manual.

Ao longo das próximas semanas, continuamos a partilhar as conversas gravadas ao vivo no @bicadosapato durante a Lisbon Design Week, reunindo algumas das vozes que estão hoje a pensar, criar e transformar o design em Portugal.

Neste episódio conversamos com Bárbara Coutinho, diretora do @mudemuseu , Ana Lia Santos, responsável pela Young Design Generation e pela ligação à comunidade académica da Lisbon Design Week, e Inês Continelli, responsável pelo Atelier Daciano da Costa.

A partir da exposição Young Design Generation e do lançamento da reedição da cadeira Osaka, refletimos sobre o papel das novas gerações, a importância da preservação da memória do design português e os desafios de transformar boas ideias em projetos sustentáveis.

Como se constrói uma cultura de design? Que responsabilidade têm os museus, as instituições e a indústria no apoio aos jovens designers? E como pode o legado de autores como Daciano da Costa continuar a inspirar quem está hoje a começar?

Uma conversa sobre continuidade, património, educação, indústria e sobre a necessidade de criar pontes entre o passado e o futuro do design português.

🎙️ Sexta é sinónimo de novo episódio do podcast Portugal Manual.

Conversas gravadas ao vivo no @bicadosapato durante a Lisbon Design Week, reunindo algumas das vozes que estão hoje a pensar, criar e transformar o design contemporâneo.

Neste episódio conversamos com a curadora @almeida_felipa , que apresentou na Lisbon Design Week a exposição na Farmácia Gomes e lançou o livro que reúne cinco anos das suas emblemáticas feiras temáticas.

Partindo deste projeto, refletimos sobre o papel da curadoria enquanto prática de investigação, mediação e construção de comunidade, e sobre a forma como uma ideia nascida durante a pandemia acabou por reunir cerca de 60 artistas ao longo de cinco anos.

Como se constrói uma linguagem curatorial reconhecível sem limitar a liberdade criativa dos artistas? Que desafios existem na valorização do trabalho artesanal contemporâneo? E o que acontece quando um projeto pensado para ser efémero decide fechar um ciclo e transformar-se?

Ao longo da conversa falamos ainda sobre coleção, memória, processos criativos, colaboração e sobre a importância de criar tempo e contexto para que o trabalho artístico possa ser verdadeiramente visto e compreendido.

Uma conversa sobre curadoria, comunidade e sobre a capacidade de um projeto criar ligações duradouras entre artistas, objetos e públicos.

E fechamos esta temporada com Michele Fajtmann fundadora da Lisbon Design Week, e @joanaastolfi designer, arquiteta e artista.

Uma conversa que parte desta última edição da Lisbon Design Week para pensar o crescimento do festival, a sua relação cada vez mais próxima com a arte e o papel que pode ter na afirmação do design português dentro e fora do país.

Falamos também da estreia do Lisbon Design Week Lounge na ARCO Lisboa pensado por Joana Astolfi como uma verdadeira sala de estar no centro da feira, reunindo mais de uma centena de peças e criando um espaço de encontro, pausa e descoberta.

Que lugar ocupa hoje o design português no contexto internacional? Como pode a colaboração entre designers, artesãos e marcas fortalecer este ecossistema? E como pode um evento independente continuar a crescer sem perder a sua identidade?

Uma conversa sobre design, cidade, colaboração e sobre o caminho que ainda temos pela frente.

Com este episódio fechamos uma temporada de 11 conversas que ficam disponíveis para ouvir no Spotify e Apple Podcasts. Se ainda não ouviram todas, aproveitem a pausa de verão para descobrir, ou revisitar, os convidados, projetos e ideias que passaram por aqui.

Em setembro voltamos. E voltamos com muitas novidades. 👀
