MEET THE MAKER | Meet Michele Grimston @michelegrimstonart, one of our artists whose exhibition is currently at the Craft + Design Canberra Gallery as part of Rewild | 2025 Artists-in-Residence Exhibition. 
.⁠
The exhibition is now on until 23 May 2026. Plan your visit to Craft + Design Canberra today. Find us upstairs above Canberra Museum and Gallery, open from Wednesday to Saturday from noon to 4pm. 
.⁠
LEARN MORE | About the Exhibition
.⁠
Rewild | Artists-in-Residence Exhibition presents new work by artists Michele Grimston @michelegrimstonart and Hannah McKellar @hannnahmckellar, developed through the 2025 Craft + Design Canberra Artist-in-Residence program at Cinerea Cottage, located within Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve. The residency combines time immersed in the landscape with a dedicated research component undertaken in partnership with the National Zoo and Aquarium @nationalzoo. 
.
Framed by the theme of Rewilding, the program invited Michele and Hannah to consider ecological restoration and shifting relationships between humans and the natural world. Through the residency’s research component with the National Zoo and Aquarium, the artists went behind the scenes to observe conservation practices and engage with rewilding as a progressive approach to conservation, one that enables natural processes to repair ecosystems and restore wilder, more biodiverse habitats. 
.
The Craft + Design Canberra Artist-in-Residence program is supported by ACT Parks and Conservation Service @actparks. The 2025 research partner was the National Zoo and Aquarium @nationalzoo.
.

STAUNCH.
This exhibition is an introduction to the STAUNCH. Collective, a collaboration presenting works created by seven Blak artists who connected through conversations about Culture as a resistance practice for/as First Peoples.  
.
Each of the artists have created work that speaks to their experiences of growth, connection and healing, opening space for discussion, discourse and joy. STAUNCH. invites you to consider what resistance truly looks like, how do you resist the colony and how do you uphold it?  
.
STAUNCH. is a cultural collective making works of art that generate Blak excellence, each artist with their own creative practice drawing from Country, Community and collaboration. 
.
STAUNCH. includes the artists Rodriguez Nalorlman Pindiying @pindiyinq (Thyemirri Bininj, Djalama Clan Group, Mamadawerre homeland, West Arnhem Land (NT)), Georgia Hoskinson 
@george.ah ( @sovereign_archive (Butchulla)), Sandy Harvey @sandycappuccino (Kalkadoon), Shanysa Jayde McConville @shanysajayde (Eastern Arrernte), Marcus Maye Wright @mayemarcuswright (Wiradjuri-Gamilaraay), Nic Ingram @nadi_yarns (Palawa and Wiradjuri ) and Maggie Douglas @maggiejean.douglas (Kabi Kabi and South Sea Islander).

LEARN MORE | About the Exhibition
.⁠
Rewild | Artists-in-Residence Exhibition presents new work by artists Michele Grimston @michelegrimstonart and Hannah McKellar @hannnahmckellar, developed through the 2025 Craft + Design Canberra Artist-in-Residence program at Cinerea Cottage, located within Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve. The residency combines time immersed in the landscape with a dedicated research component undertaken in partnership with the National Zoo and Aquarium @nationalzoo. 
.
Framed by the theme of Rewilding, the program invited Michele and Hannah to consider ecological restoration and shifting relationships between humans and the natural world. Through the residency’s research component with the National Zoo and Aquarium, the artists went behind the scenes to observe conservation practices and engage with rewilding as a progressive approach to conservation, one that enables natural processes to repair ecosystems and restore wilder, more biodiverse habitats. 
.
The Craft + Design Canberra Artist-in-Residence program is supported by ACT Parks and Conservation Service @actparks. The 2025 research partner was the National Zoo and Aquarium @nationalzoo.
.
For more information visit our website | https://craftanddesigncanberra.org/blogs/current-exhibitions/rewild-2025-artists-in-residence-exhibition
.

CONGRATULATIONS | Fuse Glass Prize 2026 Finalists Announced | Congratulations to our Members Annette Blair @annetteblairglass, Mel Douglas @meldouglasglass, Holly Grace @hollygraceartist, Kirstie Rea @reakirstie and April Widdup @made_by_april_.
.⁠
JamFactory @jamfactoryau has announced eighteen outstanding finalists that have been selected for the 2026 Fuse Glass Prize.⁠
.⁠
The judges selected the finalists from high quality and diverse entries received from artists across Australia and New Zealand. The winner of the FUSE Glass Prize Established Artist Category will receive a $20,000 non-acquisitive cash prize, with the winner of the David Henshall Emerging Artist Prize receiving a $5,000 cash prize plus a professional development opportunity at JamFactory valued at $5,000.⁠
.⁠
Brian Parkes, Chief Executive Officer at JamFactory says of the judging process that, ‘the whole panel was impressed by the quality of the entries, the calibre of the entrants, the richness of ideas and the consistently outstanding photography of the works submitted. Of course, this only made the task of selecting just twelve established and six emerging artists as finalists even more difficult! The final selection includes an exciting variety of approaches to working with glass, from leadlighting, lampworking and use of found objects to meticulous kiln-forming and virtuosic glassblowing.’ ⁠
.⁠
The exhibition of finalist’s works will be shown at JamFactory, Adelaide from 24 April - 5 July 2026 followed by the ANU School of Art & Design Gallery, Canberra from 18 August – 4 September 2026.⁠
.⁠
The winners of the Established and Emerging Categories will be announced on the 25th June 2026⁠
.⁠
To learn more visit the Fuse Glass Prize Website | https://www.fuseglassprize.com/fuse-news/2026-finalists⁠
.⁠

2026 ARTIST-IN-RESIDENCE PROGRAM IS UNDERWAY | Meet Lea Durie @lea_durie, one of three artists along with Jeffrey Sarmiento @sarmiento_glass and Julie Bartholomew @juliebartholomewceramics, who have been selected as the Craft + Design Canberra 2026 Artists-in-Residence in partnership with @nfsaonline and @actparks. 
.
In this video, hear Lea discuss how she is finding the residency so far. 
.⁠
Since 2006, we have collaborated with the ACT Parks and Conservation Service @actparks to offer residencies that explore the intersection of craft and nature. The residency provides artists with solitude and space for creative reflection, opportunities to engage in public workshops, and culminates in an exhibition at Craft + Design Canberra. ⁠
.⁠
In 2026 the research partner is the National Film and Sound Archive of Australia (NFSA) @nfsaonline, offering a two-week research period focused on Australia’s rich audiovisual heritage. Artists are now spending time at the Acton building and in the archives in Mitchell, engaging with archived voices and stories that capture our collective memories, cultural shifts and evolving identity. ⁠
.⁠
Following the research period, artists will spend three weeks at Gudgenby Ready-Cut Cottage in Namadgi National Park. Since 2006, this residency has offered a profoundly transformative environment that fosters reflection, inquiry and the development of new work. ⁠
.⁠
The residency will be followed by an Open Day at Ready-Cut Cottage in in Namadgi National Park on Saturday 28 March 2026. You can book your place now via our website by heading to craftanddesigncanberra.org and heading to the PROGRAMS page. 
.⁠
Images⁠ + Video

Sculpted by Lifestyle is a new body of work by Lee Nelms that reimagines the ‘seven deadly sins’ through an unapologetically Australian lens—less moral judgement and more reflection on how culture, habit and circumstance shape behaviour. The exhibition presents seven ‘before’ pieces that capture raw, unfiltered visages and seven amplified ‘after’ pieces that embody what those behaviours become when shaped by experience, consequence and time. 

Through hand-built and altered wheel-thrown forms, Sculpted by Lifestyle explores flaws, humour and vulnerability in both material and human nature. Expressive marks and creature-like features point to the ways lifestyle shapes us, and how we shape ourselves in return. 

@upstageingcanberra Festival
Visit the exhibition at the Craft + Design Canberra Gallery⁠, upstairs in the North Building, 180 London Circuit Canberra⁠
Open Wednesday to Saturday, Noon to 4pm⁠, To 28 March.

ON NOW | Sculpted By Lifestyle by Lee Nelms @nelmsie2022 until 28 March 2026. Visit Craft + Design Canberra to see the works in person.⁠
.⁠
Sculpted by Lifestyle is a new body of work by Lee Nelms that reimagines the 'seven deadly sins' through an unapologetically Australian lens—less moral judgement and more reflection on how culture, habit and circumstance shape behaviour. The exhibition presents seven ‘before’ pieces that capture raw, unfiltered visages and seven amplified ‘after’ pieces that embody what those behaviours become when shaped by experience, consequence and time. ⁠
.⁠
Through hand-built and altered wheel-thrown forms, Sculpted by Lifestyle explores flaws, humour and vulnerability in both material and human nature. Expressive marks and creature-like features point to the ways lifestyle shapes us, and how we shape ourselves in return. ⁠
.⁠
Visit the exhibition at the Craft + Design Canberra Gallery⁠. Open Wednesday to Saturday, Noon to 4pm⁠, upstairs in the North Building, 180 London Circuit Canberra⁠
.⁠
View the catalogue and buy the work online via our website via the link in our bio.⁠

This book was a wild ride, start to finish. ⁠

A story of guilt, secrets, classism, sexism and redemption — that begs the question, what would you give for success? ⁠

This book is for the psychological thriller lovers — it’s a true whodunnit that keeps you guessing cover to cover. ⁠

20 YEARS AGO | est. 2005 by Phoebe Porter and Blanche Tilden @blanchetilden @phoebe.porter.⁠
.⁠
Let's take a moment to look back twenty years and see what Craft + Design Canberra was doing in 2006.⁠ Twenty years ago, Accredited Professional Member of Craft + Design Canberra Phoebe Porter and Blanche Tilden exhibited at our Gallery in Civic. ⁠
.⁠
Blanche Tilden & Phoebe Porter recently provided the following quote, reflecting on their partnership and exhibition.⁠
.⁠
'Thinking back to ‘Est 2005’, we appreciate the significant role Craft + Design Canberra has played and continues to play in fostering new talent, creating opportunities, building community and connecting emerging and established craftspeople and designers.'⁠
.⁠
'Encouraged by the then Director, Barb McConchie, and supported by funding by the Australia Council, ‘Est 2005’ was the outcome of a mentorship and acted as a springboard for our shared workshop 'Studio Hacienda'. Following ‘Est 2005’, we continued to work together on ambitious projects, presenting our work at ‘Smartworks: Design and the Handmade’ at the Powerhouse Museum, and receiving a Victorian Premier’s Design Award for our collaborative jewellery project, ‘General Assembly’.'⁠
.⁠
Here is a short excerpt from Jas Hugonnet, essay writer about the partnership. ⁠
'In August 2005 Phoebe Porter, an emerging jeweller from Canberra, traveled to Melbourne to undertake a three month mentorship with jeweller, Blanche Tilden in her Fitzroy studio. During this time Porter worked closely with Tilden to develop and produce a number of pieces for Tilden's Carte Blanche exhibition.'⁠
.⁠

@jamfactoryau JamFactory’s ICON series celebrates the achievements of South Australia’s most influential visual artists working in craft-based media. With a practice spanning 35 years, Julie Blyfield is a jeweller and metalsmith who is renowned for her intricately crafted jewellery and sculptural objects that capture the essence of the Australian landscape. ⁠
.⁠
Often referencing specimens found in natural history collections, as well as those she collects herself in nature, Blyfield’s jewellery and objects take inspiration from the forms, textures and patterns of Australian botanicals, plants and marine life. ⁠

2026 Craft + Design Canberra Emerging Contemporaries
Artists | Giselle Bailie Anderson, Sarah Brown, Nina Casey-Brown, Jake Haynes, Tessa Hoser, Liv Kidston, Isaac Kozlovskis, Ingrid McGrouther, Campbell Miller, Jenn Morton, Eliott June O’Dowd, Zali Odlum, Paloma Padovan, Luc Puchert, Rosalie Ryan, Lisa Stevenson and Mulloon Institute Design Project (Eddie Condé, Oonagh O’Dwyer, Kayla Wade-Lehman and Anne Wen)

Exhibition Statement 
2026 Craft + Design Canberra Emerging Contemporaries is Craft + Design Canberra’s prestigious award exhibition celebrating the next generation of designers and makers. Showcasing works by early career artists from leading local institutions, this exhibition highlights the diverse talent shaping the future of craft and design. 
.
JamFactory ICON Julie Blyfield: Chasing a Passion @julieblyfield @jamfactoryau 
.
Exhibition Statement 
JamFactory’s ICON series celebrates the achievements of South Australia’s most influential visual artists working in craft-based media. With a practice spanning 35 years, Julie Blyfield is a jeweller and metalsmith who is renowned for her intricately crafted jewellery and sculptural objects that capture the essence of the Australian landscape. Often referencing specimens found in natural history collections, as well as those she collects herself in nature. 
.
Sculpted by Lifestyle by Lee Nelms @nelmsie2022 
.
Exhibition Statement 
.
Sculpted by Lifestyle is a new body of work by Lee Nelms that reimagines the ‘seven deadly sins’ through an unapologetically Australian lens—less moral judgement and more reflection on how culture, habit and circumstance shape behaviour.
.

May Book Club picks are here!⁠

Join the Byron Writers Festival team — Lex and Jas — this May and read along with two standout titles.⁠

Flashlight by Susan Choi⁠
Shortlisted for the prestigious 2025 Booker Prize, Flashlight has emerged as one of the most talked-about novels on this year’s list. It tells the extraordinary story of a family shaped by the currents of the twentieth century, moving between Japan, the United States, and the North Korean regime.⁠
⁠
Two Hundred Million Musketeers by Ender Başkın⁠
Shortlisted for the Victorian Premier's Literary Awards, this powerful poetry collection explores the complexities of new parenthood, family life, and the quiet anxieties about the world future generations will inherit.⁠
⁠
Pick up a copy from your local bookstore and read along with us this May.⁠

THIRTY YEARS AGO | Tags, an exhibition of contemporary jewellery was shown in 1996 at Craft + Design Canberra (then Craft ACT).⁠
.⁠
Let's take a moment to look back thirty years and see what was happening at Craft + Design Canberra in 1996. ⁠
.⁠
Thirty years ago, we were so fortunate to have work by Mari Funaki @funakigallery, Rowena Gough @rowena.gough, Marian Hosking @hoskingmarian, Yuri Kawanabe, Andrew Last, Sue Lorraine @sue__lorraine, Carlier Makigawa @carlier_makigawa, Mascha Moje @mascha.moje, Catherine Truman @catherinetruman and David Walker @ainswalk. The exhibition, tags, was curated by Helen Aitken Kuhnen @aitkenkuhnen. ⁠
.⁠
The exhibition ran from 4 to 29 September 1996 and was opened by Grace Cochrane at our Watson location.⁠
.⁠
The catalogue shares that 'tags is an exhibition of contemporary jewellery by some of the most respected makers in Australia. In the context of the exhibition tags is a personal identification or signature, much the same as a dog tag is to a soldier. Like a maker's mark, be it a signature or metal stamping, the piece sin tags convey a recognisable style and workmanship.'⁠
.⁠
'Australia has some of the best contemporary jewellers in the world. tags showcases the unique approaches of a recognisably Australian style'.⁠
.⁠
It is incredibly inspiring to see where these jewellers are today, and wonderful to have had two back in the gallery only last year with @catherinetruman and @sue__lorraine part of Beautiful Tensions: Gray Street Workshop Celebrates Forty Years by @jamfactoryau. Even the catalogue is a work of art.⁠
.⁠
Did you attend or view this exhibition in 1996? Do you have any more information or photos of the work?⁠
.⁠

20 YEARS AGO | Simply Cloth by Monique van Nieuwland @moniquevnieuwland. 
.⁠
Let's take a moment to look back twenty years and see what Craft + Design Canberra was doing in 2006.⁠
.⁠
Twenty years ago, Accredited Professional Member Monique van Nieuwland exhibited these remarkable works in her solo exhibition at Craft + Design Canberra. This year, she returned to exhibit in our 2025 Annual Members Exhibition. We're fortunate to have world-class makers like Monique as part of our community, continuing to create and share their craft with us across the decades.⁠
.⁠
'Monique’s last solo exhibition of hand woven work: “simply cloth”, looked at simple and ordinary textiles. The installation showed the beauty of everyday textiles (such as handkerchiefs, dishcloths, nappies, washers, tea towels, blankets) evoking personal stories and memories. The work addressed environmental concerns, highlighting wasteful practices in Western societies, where ordinary and utilitarian woven cloth is disappearing, substituted by synthetic and disposable alternatives.' - Networks Australia via https://networksaustralia.blogspot.com/2011/05/monique-van-nieuwland.html⁠
.⁠
ABOUT MONIQUE | Accredited Professional Member of Craft + Design Canberra⁠
.⁠
Monique van Nieuwland learned to weave in the Netherlands and bought her first loom in the late 70s while she was working on a commission weaving fabrics for curtains and tablecloths. After migrating to Australia in 1982, Monique studied Visual Arts-Textiles at the Australian National University School of Art and has completed her masters degree.⁠
.⁠
LEARN MORE | Visit our Members Directory via our website to learn more about Monique van Nieuwland⁠ @moniquevnieuwland.
.⁠
Images | Artworks by Monique van Nieuwland as part of her exhibition Simply Cloth at Craft + Design Canberra | Photography by Creative Image Photography

10 YEARS AGO | Grow Your Own by Amanda Dziedzic @amanda_dziedzic, Danielle Rickaby @_yo.dan_, Lauren Simeoni @laurensimeoni and Melinda Young⁠ @unnaturaljeweller. Exhibition text by @pottypryor. 
.⁠
Let's take a moment to look back ten years and see what Craft + Design Canberra was doing in 2016.⁠
.⁠
Shown in the Craft + Design Canberra Gallery across September and October in 2016, Grow Your Own explored the idea of 'the greenhouse', an intimate indoor space providing a fertile background for four makers working in diverse mediums who cultivate, cross-pollinate and present exciting new works in a captivating environment. ⁠
.⁠
All the artists shared a common love of the garden and the natural world which manifests into their aesthetic and conceptual practices.⁠
.⁠

Shree's novel Tomb of Sand made literary history in 2022 as the first work written in Hindi, or any Indian language, to win the International Booker Prize.⁠

INTO THE ARCHIVE | Gallery Calendar from 1973.⁠
.⁠
Craft + Design Canberra is fortunate to have catalogues and records from the beginning of our organisation and through it's first decade. During 1973, President John Scolley and the committee published the August newsletter, featuring this gallery calendar.⁠
.⁠
The gallery calendar showcases the breadth and depth of craftspeople across Canberra and beyond. It also features an artwork by Peter Travis (1929 - 2016) who the National Gallery of Australia describes as 'an industrial designer, ceramicist, kite-maker, swimwear designer, colour consultant and teacher' and was the designer of the famous swimwear item, the Speedo. ⁠
.⁠
Do you recognise any names on this list? Were you lucky enough to attend any of these exhibitions?⁠
.⁠

Image | Gallery Calendar in the Craft Association of the Australian Capital Territory Newsletter Volume 2, Number 3 August 1973 | Photography by Craft + Design Canberra Staff

This memoir tells the story of a young woman who grows up carrying an unnamed sadness long before she has the language to understand it, exploring universal themes of trauma, attachment, grief, sexuality, motherhood, and the ways women learn to survive by becoming psychologically invisible. It opens with the death of the author’s brother, protector and emotional refuge, a loss that fractures the illusion of a happy family life and forces a confrontation with hidden pain that shaped the family long before his death. 

Structured in three parts, it traces the author’s journey from psychological fragmentation toward healing, through psychiatric medication, therapy, spirituality, and radical self-examination, finally arriving at the act of accepting her pain rather than escaping it, and asking whether joy is possible after surviving so long inside it.

Memoar ini menceritakan kisah seorang perempuan muda yang tumbuh dengan membawa kesedihan tanpa nama jauh sebelum ia memiliki bahasa untuk memahaminya, mengeksplorasi tema-tema universal tentang trauma, keterikatan, duka, seksualitas, keibuan, dan cara-cara perempuan belajar bertahan hidup dengan menjadi tak terlihat secara psikologis. Kisah ini dibuka dengan kematian saudara laki-laki sang penulis, pelindung dan tempat berlindung emosionalnya, sebuah kehilangan yang meruntuhkan ilusi kehidupan keluarga yang bahagia dan memaksa konfrontasi dengan luka tersembunyi yang telah membentuk keluarga jauh sebelum kematiannya. 

Tersusun dalam tiga bagian, memoar ini menelusuri perjalanan sang penulis dari kehancuran psikologis menuju penyembuhan, melalui obat-obatan psikiatri, terapi, spiritualitas, dan penelusuran diri yang radikal, hingga akhirnya sampai pada tindakan menerima rasa sakitnya alih-alih menghindarinya, sembari bertanya apakah kebahagiaan masih mungkin setelah begitu lama bertahan di dalam luka.

.⁠
Today we honour F!nk + Co, a much loved and respected Australian design company with an international reputation for producing world-class tableware, jewellery, lighting and more.⁠
.⁠
ABOUT F!NK + CO⁠
F!NK + Co. was established by Robert Foster in 1993 in Queanbeyan, NSW, Australia, with the aim of creating a design and manufacturing business that would support and generate opportunities for Australian designer-makers. Joined by Gretel Harrison in 1995, together they built F!NK + Co. into the business it is today – a much loved and respected Australian design company with an international reputation for producing world-class tableware, hollowware, jewellery and lighting.⁠
.⁠
Be it the iconic F!NK Water Jug, the squashed Storage Vessels, the graceful Coolamon Platters, the Ned Kelly-esque Wine Chiller or the subtle curves of the Beaker, every F!NK product melds refined craftsmanship with shapes and colours largely inspired by the Australian landscape – tropical corals, fish and anemones, endless blue skies and vast ancient deserts.⁠

caption:
MINE(ral).
Lisbon Design Week 2026.
Studio : Gameiro x ST VINCENTS x Nick Valentijn. 
A Mine. Seen and sensed, and studied.

Over the last years our Studio has celebrated something which is very close to our hearts: empirical evidence.
Besides all the usual theories and talks, and the research process which is essential to clear our minds, it’s a fact that you can’t beat experience. 
As we set to do something unique for LDW26, it was also clear that if we named our exhibition and installation MINE(ral), we really needed to go down a mine.
What you see here is a bridge, factual and efficient, but also mesmerizing in its magical reach, which we established with the Boliden Neves-Corvo Mine.
As we went down its tunnels and galleries, and as we met the people who work above and underground, it would be impossible not to “save” that visual (and audio) experience for our records and archive.
We tend to forget that everything which we use on the surface, daily, usually comes from deep underground.
As it is, this is a reminder, and a thank-you note, to all those you don’t usually see. 
This is the light at the end of the tunnel. 
How beautiful is that?
Thank you to our dear friend Pedro Zavial for the extraordinary video.
Please join us with ST VINCENTS and Nick Valentijn during Lisbon Design Week at our Studio from May the 27th to the 31st.
Frida (a truly shiny dog) will be our golden nugget.

2026 ARTIST-IN-RESIDENCE ANNOUNCED | Craft + Design Canberra is thrilled to announce that Jeffrey Sarmiento @sarmiento_glass, Julie Bartholomew @juliebartholomewceramics and Lea Durie @lea_durie have been selected as the 2026 Artists-in-Residence. ⁠
.⁠
This competitive program undergoes a rigorous review by a committee of Accredited Professional Members of Craft + Design Canberra, representing diverse craft and design mediums. ⁠
.⁠
For 19 years, we have collaborated with the ACT Parks and Conservation Service @actparks to offer residencies that explore the intersection of craft and nature. The residency provides artists with solitude and space for creative reflection, opportunities to engage in public workshops, and culminates in an exhibition at Craft + Design Canberra. ⁠
.⁠
In 2026 the research partner will be the National Film and Sound Archive of Australia (NFSA) @nfsaonline, offering a two-week research period focused on Australia’s rich audiovisual heritage. During this period, artists will engage with archived voices and stories that capture our collective memories, cultural shifts and evolving identity. ⁠
.⁠
Following the research period, artists will spend three weeks at Gudgenby Ready-Cut Cottage in Namadgi National Park. Since 2006, this residency has offered a profoundly transformative environment that fosters reflection, inquiry and the development of new work. ⁠
.⁠
The residency will be followed by an Open Day at Ready-Cut Cottage in in Namadgi National Park on Saturday 28 March 2026, where the artists will host creative workshops. Stay tuned for more details so you don't miss this exciting opportunity to take part. ⁠
.⁠
Congratulations to Jeffrey, Julie and Lea! ⁠
.⁠
Read more via our website | Click the NEWS link in our bio.⁠
.⁠

FIRE COUNTRY | Be safe and stay cool this weekend. Our thoughts are with all those affected across Australia. 
.
These works were part of the Fire Country exhibition by @becselleck and James Taylor, a furniture and photography installation addressing the physical and cultural significance of fire in Australia, that was displayed at Craft + Design Canberra in 2022. 
.
The artists wrote that ‘These works are representative of our
contemporary relationship with fire and potential for better engagement in the future.’
.
‘Comprising a living room and dining setting, the furniture pieces are made from Australian Eucalypt timber species burnt to carbon black, sealed with animal fats, and inlaid with polished bronze casts of new leaf shoots and post-fire fungi. The surrounding gallery hang of black and white imagery on burnt timber frames features photographs taken from various ecosystems in NSW, ACT and SA that have experienced catastrophic fires in recent years.’
.
‘Fire Country attempts to embrace fire in Australia as a part of our collective culture. Referencing the symbiotic relationship that fire has with our continent’s landscapes, the work captures the intrinsic beauty of this interplay through the iconic Eucalyptus.’
.
‘Through this series of furniture and photography we want to offer not just sorrow for what we’ve lost, but also hope for our future.’
.
Images | Works by Rebeca Selleck and James Taylor as part of the Fire Country exhibition at Craft + Design Canberra in 2022 | Photography by 5 Foot Photgraphy

This is the story of Aditi’s journey from burnout and self-abandonment towards inner alignment, a deeply personal and timely exploration of the courage it takes to begin again. After experiencing the quiet unravelling that so often accompanies burnout, she confronts the ways she has been living out of sync with herself: over-giving, overworking, and overlooking her own needs. 

Through storytelling, reflection and grounded guidance, she invites readers into the often uncomfortable, yet transformative space of slowing down, reconnecting with the body, and learning to trust their own voice again, offering a new paradigm: that doing less is not failure, but a radical act of choosing a life that feels aligned and true.

📍 Rumah Kayu at Taman Baca Ubud
🗓️ Friday, 23 October
⏰ 1.15 PM

Ini adalah kisah perjalanan Aditi dari burnout dan pengabaian diri menuju keselarasan batin, sebuah eksplorasi yang sangat personal dan relevan tentang keberanian untuk memulai kembali. Setelah mengalami keruntuhan perlahan yang kerap menyertai burnout, ia dihadapkan pada kenyataan bahwa selama ini ia hidup tidak selaras dengan dirinya sendiri: terlalu banyak memberi, terlalu keras bekerja, dan mengabaikan kebutuhannya sendiri. 

Melalui kisah personal, refleksi, dan panduan yang membumi, ia mengajak pembaca memasuki ruang yang sering kali tidak nyaman, namun transformatif, untuk melambat, terhubung kembali dengan tubuh, dan belajar memercayai suara hatinya sendiri, menawarkan sebuah paradigma baru: bahwa melakukan lebih sedikit bukanlah kegagalan, melainkan tindakan radikal untuk memilih hidup yang selaras dan autentik.

Rising Sparks is a grassroots collective creating spaces where the next generation can come together, steward a living culture, and build something that belongs to them — rooted in sustainability and care for the world they’re inheriting.

📸: “Our Ouroboros” by Youtian Duan and Kai Zhang

With mentorship, resources, and a global community to support, Rising Sparks exists to inspire a world where participatory, non-commercial culture belongs to everyone who cultivates it — carried forward by diverse communities rooted in authentic connection, collective stewardship, creative self-expression, and regenerative ways of living.

📸: @splinter.photography

In our first year, Rising Sparks hosted community-run gatherings across major US cities, connected 800+ community members into the global mycelium network of Burning Man 🍄, distributed $10K in grants to next-gen collectives of artists, leaders and changemakers, and helped 120+ emerging artists and leaders find their way to Black Rock City. This is just the beginning.

📸: “Our Ouroboros” by Youtian Duan and Kai Zhang

If you’re new to Burning Man, want to shift from consumer to creator, and feel the pull, this is your invite. If you are a seasoned change maker, innovator, artist or leader who wants to help carry it forward, this is your place too. Rising Sparks is where it starts. Burning Man has always been built by the people who show up and make something

.⁠
Please join us to celebrate the launch of Fallen Leaves by Rebecca Selleck at Namadgi Visitor Centre. ⁠
.⁠
About the Launch | Saturday 6 December 2025⁠
Artist Talk | From 11am ⁠
Official Launch | From 11.30am ⁠
Location | Namadgi Visitor Centre, Naas Rd, Tharwa ACT 2620 ⁠
RSVP | Free event. RSVP essential via the link in bio.⁠
.⁠
ABOUT THE ARTWORK⁠
Fallen Leaves was commissioned by Craft + Design Canberra in partnership with ACT Parks and Conservation @actparks. This site-specific artwork by Canberra-based artists Rebecca Selleck, responds to the theme 'Fire in the Landscape’ and is a reflection on the evolving impact of climate change and the increasing severity of weather events in the ACT region. ⁠
.⁠
ARTWORK STATEMENT⁠
The Orroral Valley bushfire was so big and close we could see it from our backyard. I had my newborn in my arms. I could feel the thousands of choked breaths and splintering of great limbs as ecosystems collapsed. I was scared for my child’s future. For all our kids’ futures. ⁠
 .⁠
The land wasn’t recognisable. The fires were so hot they destroyed too much. But still the charred eucalypts shot out their epicormic growth. Along with other devastating fires around Australia, the Orroral Valley fire was the catalyst for intensifying conversations across the country around climate change and human impact. ⁠
 .⁠
For those of us who choose to remember, we go on with sorrow in our hearts and hope for the future. This artwork is a reminder. On a granite boulder, a child lays, tenderly touching the hand of a kangaroo joey. These figures are both at rest, facing towards Mount Tennent. Curved over them is the blackened bronze form of a burnt young eucalypt still in the act of sheltering, and below their young leaves form a glistening bed. ⁠
.⁠
Images | Rebecca Selleck Fallen Leaves 2025 | Photography by Rebecca Selleck⁠
.⁠

It was genuinely such a delight documenting this year’s @northcoastceramics Mud Trail. This is an event in which over 30 incredible ceramic artists open their studios to visitors across the Northern Rivers over 4 days. I couldn't tell you how many times I've seen Built To Spill over the last 30 years. Last night's @pickathon set was the second time I've seen them in the past few weeks and they're playing another one at the festival tonight. Somehow, it never gets old and the energy this time was as palpable as ever. Cherry Hill was packed with the crowd "spilling" out around the sides and back of the stage.

The last time BTS played Pickathon was 2022, the same year their last album was released. There's no new LP to promote, but it doesn't seem to matter. 34 years after the project's formation, they appear to be more popular than ever. The front of the stage was full of a new generation of fans being raised on this music demonstrating the same overwhelming love for them as all of us old heads. The crowd was singing along. These kids know the words and feel them.

This isn't the type of singing from the crowd where you just want others to see you so you can pull focus. It's not about going louder than the speakers or hoping the band members or others in attendance notice you're hitting every word, so as to assert some delusional dominance within your fandom. This was the far rarer crowd singalong, where nobody from the stage prompts you and the voices are actually welcome among others, because you are just one of many in a wobbly chorus. It's not only forgivable, but welcomed, because it just pours out of you. It's uncontainable. The singing may not always be harmonious, but the energy was.

These aren't Doug's songs anymore. At this point, he's more like a mystic preacher or shaman with some electric weapon there to deliver psalms from the collective cultural and spiritual history. The sound and tales are intoxicating, swirling through the atmosphere like ether. 

The world is broken, but the kids are all right. If nothing else, Built To Spill makes it feels like there's a chance we all could be. It's why we come out. It feels good to believe that a new wave will continue to keep it alive. It feels good to believe in anything and know it's justified.

What happens after a ceramic kiln burns continuously for 100 hours? 🔥🏺 

Participants witnessed the reveal last month at an anagama kiln opening during the celebrated North Coast Mud Trail. Jo Norton, ceramic artist and Technical Assistant at TAFE NSW Murwillumbah, supported the event, having assisted with the construction of the anagama kiln. 

Hosted at Middle Pocket Pottery by acclaimed ceramic artist and TAFE NSW Lismore graduate Venessa Stella Skye, the hands-on experience offered visitors a unique opportunity to explore traditional wood-firing techniques and connect with the thriving ceramics community of the Northern Rivers. 🤎🧑‍🎨🪵

For Jo, woodfiring is a key part of her own ceramic practice and a rewarding opportunity to share her knowledge of this unique firing process.

It's just one of the many ways TAFE NSW staff stay connected with industry and bring contemporary practices and insights back to the classroom, helping students develop skills that work. 📚

Attempting to demonstrate throwing off the hump at the Mud Trail on Sunday.
I moved the wheel from the studio to outside the kitchen doors to save people traipsing all the way over there, possibly in the rain.
I first saw throwing off the hump in India in 1967 on the way back from England after my mother’s funeral.
She had been making pottery for a few months before her untimely demise and I inherited a couple of pieces. I was touched to have these tangible reminders of her and that was the trigger for me starting making pottery a few years back.
After I left parliament, I started to do it again more seriously and have saved well over fifty thousand acres of rainforest with the proceeds.
This photograph was taken, fittingly, by my granddaughter Bodhi, who has also become a ceramicist with her partner Corey and she uses my mother pottery tools. They make fabulous pieces. Life continues.

Surrounded by monuments, palaces and a park that overlooks the Tejo river, Santa Clara 1728 stands as the city sanctuary. Bearing the touch of architect Manuel Aires Mateus and interior by @ama_mrp, the hotel’s architectural language is soft and serene, defined by a respect for space and void. 

𝗔𝘁 𝗟𝗗𝗪‘𝟮𝟲
Santa Clara 1728 opens its doors to present an exhibition by Malga ceramic. Rooted in traditional techniques and reinterpreted through a contemporary lens, Malga’s work reflects a quiet dialogue between craft heritage and modern living. The exhibition is not a simple gallery display, instead the ceramics are integrated throughout the hotel’s space, on tables, shelves and in everyday settings. 
During the Week, the restaurant Solo invites guests to linger and enjoy a light lunch menu, served on the very ceramics displayed in the exhibition. Solo is open from Tuesday to Saturday (12:30–15:30) offering an opportunity to experience contemporary ceramics in the most natural setting, in use, at the table.

For bookings contact the venue.

Based in Lisbon, Studio Mirante is a multi-disciplinary atelier founded by artists Margaux Carel and Clotilde de Kersauson. The studio is rooted in ceramics, but artists from diverse disciplines are welcomed here to collaborate, experiment and contaminate each other's ideas. 

𝗔𝘁 𝗟𝗗𝗪‘𝟮𝟲
Studio Mirante invites Pangea: the exhibition responds to complexity and noise by creating a space of poetry and reflection. "In the Dreamtime, the ancestors travelled from Inkwareny (honey ant place) to Ilpereny (North Pine Hill station). Anmatyerr, Alyawarr and Warlpiri people share this Inkwareny (honeyant) Anengkerr (dreaming) connected to different significant places."

“They came back to Yuelamu. From Yuelamu, they went to Yuendumu and past Yuendumu. They got wet and got to Wanukurru-parnta (the tree is named Wanukurru), and they returned to Yuelumu. They lived here. All of them were women.”

This piece, 'The Barramundi Dreaming' is by artist Zachary Stack from @WarmunArt Centre.

"Inspired by the Barramundi Dreaming story shared with Zachary Stack by his great-grandmother, the late Gija artist Lena Nyadbi OAM. Carrying forward this important Ngarrangkarni (Dreamtime), Zachary presents the story through his own artistic voice while honouring the cultural knowledge passed down through his family. 

The repeated white forms represent the scales of the barramundi, scattered across Country. The clustered forms represent the place where the Argyle Diamond Mine was established. 

In Gija tradition, this Country carries an ancient Dreaming, where the barramundi’s scales became the pink diamonds found within the land. 

The story ia a reminder that Country holds a much deeper history, one that has existed since the beginning of the time. Surrounding this place are the Ancestors, whose presence continues to watch over and protect the land. Their enduring connection to Country reflects the strength of Gija Law, culture, and Ngarrangkarni, reminding us that these stories remain alive and continue to guide future generations. 

Through this painting, Zachary honours his family’s artistic legacy while sharing Gija stories in his own emerging voice. His work reflects the enduring relationship between Ancestors, Country, and culture, carrying forward the knowledge entrusted to him by his Elders for generations to come."

𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴 @vascofm at @thelisbonaire

The Lisbonaire is a design-led residence housed in a renovated 1960s building, known for integrating Portuguese art, typography and architecture into everyday living. Extending this ethos below ground, its basement offers an intimate and atmospheric setting for exhibitions and cultural gatherings during Lisbon Design Week. 

𝗔𝘁 𝗟𝗗𝗪‘𝟮𝟲
Framed by The Lisbonaire’s basement, Vasco Fragoso Mendes presents an exhibition that traces his evolution as an artist, designer and maker. This piece, Kungkarrangkalpa (Seven Sisters) – Wanarn, is by artist Joy Nginana Lyons from @PapulankutjaArtists.

"The painting depicts the Wanarn chapter of the Kungkarrangkalpa (Seven Sisters) Tjukurrpa, an important women’s story travelling across the Ngaanyatjarra Lands and wider Western Desert.

Along this section of the songline, the sisters flee eastward across Country while being pursued by Yurla (Wati Nyiru), a powerful ancestral man associated with the constellation Orion. In the Wanarn region the sisters are known as Kungkarrangkalpa, meaning “many sisters”, and the story is carried through significant rock formations, caves, waterholes and ceremonial sites that remain visible in the landscape today.

As the sisters travel through places such as Tjitjipirnitjunku, Kunangurra, Wilurrampal and Kungkarrangkal, Yurla continues chasing them, attempting to trap and capture them. He hides in caves, watches from the hills and uses magic and trickery to pursue the women across the desert. At Kunangurra the sisters shelter in a cave before flying onward to escape him once again.

The Wanarn songline holds deep cultural significance for Ngaanyatjarra families connected to this Country. The story maps both ancestral events and living kinship ties across generations. The rockholes, hills, caves and trees throughout the landscape are understood as evidence of the sisters’ travels and the actions of Yurla during the Tjukurrpa.

Today the story continues to be told through painting, song, dance and travel on Country. Artists paint these places not only as remembered ancestral sites, but as living cultural landscapes connected to family, law and identity."

Words courtesy of Papulankutja Artists.

What began with four main works (a light box by Jeff Wall, a self-portrait by Cindy Sherman, a view of Shanghai by Thomas Struth and an image of a bookcase by Candida Höfer), the novobanco Photography Collection has rapidly grown into an archive of over 1000 works. The Collection, curated from the beginning by art advisor Alexandra Fonseca Pinho, became publicly accessible in 2008. 

𝗔𝘁 𝗟𝗗𝗪‘𝟮𝟲
novobanco Photography Gallery hosts “Terra”: terracotta sculptures crafted by Beatriz Horta Correia dialogue with photographs personally chosen by the artists from the novobanco collection. Here, clay is both matter and metaphor, reflecting ancestral practices and a rhythm that connects human beings to their environments. The photographs continue this reflection, opening new perspectives on how land is lived. 

The exhibition is complemented by textiles of @bombony__ and a video installation by @miguelffgaspar.

Meet our next teacher for the 5th edition of the Wander Yogi Festival. 🌿 Joana Cadete 

Joana is passionate about family, yoga, surf, and nature — which is why she calls Ericeira home where she has her own yoga studio since 2009. Deeply rooted in the Ashtanga tradition, she had the privilege of studying for several years at the KPJAYI in Mysore with Sri K. Felipa Almeida is a curator and art director specializing in the intersection of art, crafts and Portuguese material culture and traditions. In 2020 she established a creative studio in Lisbon where she collaborates with artists and artisans. She curates exhibitions, bespoke projects and collections. Almeida’s exhibition takes place at the historic Farmácia Gomes, former laboratory and place of practice.

𝗔𝘁 𝗟𝗗𝗪‘𝟮𝟲
Felipa presents the result of a five-year cycle marked by 11 thematic fairs held in her Studio. This journey is celebrated through an exhibition that brings together around 60 artists as part of a collective show. Alongside, she launches her new “Book of Fairs”, born from the desire to give presence to an ephemeral world and gather memories and collaborations.

Why this theme, why now?

The world is witnessing a very dark period in history, and for a long time I felt so powerless and helpless. No matter what I would do, I would always feel that it wasn't enough. And I couldn't find any solution.
But then I came across a video of Jane Goodall, where she said: "You cannot get through a single day without having an impact on the world around you. What you do makes a difference, and you have to decide what kind of difference you want to make."
That stayed with me.
And then I found another quote of hers that hit just as hard: "Every individual matters. Every individual has a role to play. Every individual makes a difference."
That is when something shifted.
We can always start from the people around us — from our community, our neighbours, the person next to us on the mat. Small acts of connection matter. Showing up for each other matters. Creating spaces where people feel less alone matters.
And that is exactly what the Wander Yogi has always tried to do. This year, with The Invisible Thread as our theme, we want to go deeper into that idea. Yoga means union — and union is not just a concept we explore in philosophy class. It is something we can live, practice, and offer to the world every single day.

We cannot solve everything. But we can choose what kind of difference we make ✨

With love,
Carlotta
Founder, The Wander Yogi

The night is threefold:

⭒ A place: Fahrenheit.works design pieces are presented alongside a new collaborative work developed specifically with Wasted Time.
⭒ A materiality: furniture crafted entirely from 100% biomaterials, utilizing algae and oyster shells recovered directly from the food industry.

caption:
Behind every finished pot is a series of not so glamorous steps and a heck of a lot of time waiting. Here are the pots drying after being washed as they come out of their first firing. I always love this scene as the sun dances across their bottoms. 

I wait, I wax the bottoms, I wait, I mix up and apply glazes, I wait, I clean the bases, I load them in the kiln very carefully, and then they get fired.

Again, I wait, I unload the kiln, I sand each base, I wash each pot and then finally they are ready. 

Each pot is handled carefully and lovingly through this whole process and it’s kind of daunting thinking of it like this. But it’s always worth it in the end ✨

We are very excited to share this year's Festival topic: The Invisible thread, what connects us all 🕉

Yoga means union. A word that has never felt more necessary.

In times of division and uncertainty, we need to be reminded of what we share. Yoga has always known that beneath our differences — our stories, our struggles, our borders — there is something that connects us all. A common ground. A shared humanity. A breath that belongs to no one and to everyone.

This October, we come together to explore that connection. On the mat and off it. Within ourselves and with each other.

Because the practice of yoga is not just personal. It is, at its heart, an act of peace. ☮

𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴 @mudemuseu

MUDE - Museu do Design is Lisbon’s public municipal museum dedicated to design in all its expressions. The Museum Collection, which currently has 19 major collections and 5 nuclei (Scene, Graphics, Contemporary Jewellery, Fashion & Product), has been growing, giving priority to the preservation, study and dissemination of design in Portugal, as well as the incorporation of archives. 

𝗔𝘁 𝗟𝗗𝗪‘𝟮𝟲
MUDE hosts the LDW'26 Young Design Generation Open Call Exhibition, showcasing the work of the 20 finalists. From My City (FMC), organising entity of Lisbon Design Week, partners with MUDE with a focus on the YDG initiative, an open call by LDW aimed at supporting the new generation of designers in Portugal. 
One piece presented through the open call and selected by the jury will be incorporated into MUDE’s collection, alongside an awarding of a mentorship program. 
YDG also benefits from the support of @novobanco , sponsor of LDW since its inception.  Open to participants under the age of 35, this open audition celebrates the creativity, experimentation and diversity of young Portuguese designers or those living in Portugal, giving visibility to projects that reflect the transformations of contemporary design as a cultural, social and ecological practice.

Two designers working in the same street in Ajuda join forces in a collaboration that brings together ceramics and jewellery. Mafalda Girão is a contemporary jewellery atelier founded in 2018 as a personal extension of its creator’s inner world: raw metal is shaped, refined and transformed into objects that carry presence and meaning. Pareidólia Design, founded by Tatiana Ferreira, is a ceramics studio dedicated to the exploration of form, texture and storytelling.

𝗔𝘁 𝗟𝗗𝗪‘𝟮𝟲
The Practice of the Gesture: A Distributed Body. This collaboration emerges as an unfolding across two neighboring studios to explore the threshold between ceramic forms and metal elements. This limited collection, formed by two coffee tables and two boxes, approaches the object not as a static ornament but as a functional site of interaction.

From the bold storytelling of Doris Bush Nungarrayi, to the rich cultural narratives of Nola Campbell and Betty Campbell, this year’s Darwin Aboriginal Art Fair (DAAF) celebrates the extraordinary depth and diversity of First Nations art.

Each work carries generations of knowledge, memory and connection to Country, offering a glimpse into stories that have been shared and preserved for tens of thousands of years. It’s a privilege to experience these works and to support the incredible artists and communities behind them.

If you’re visiting DAAF this year, take your time with each piece. There is so much to discover beyond the canvas.

Constanca Entrudo atelier functions as a design studio, production space and material experimentation laboratory, where textile research is combined with manual practice and collaboration with industry. DC.AD is a studio founded in 2014 by Duarte Caldas which focuses on architecture, interiors, furniture and light design: each space is enhanced by unique, bespoke solutions.

Each piece is made up of two layers, a modular transparent acrylic structure and a printed or plain textile covering, exploring different levels of transparency, density and texture.

From the East of the Torres Strait to Larrakia Country. 

I sat down with Annretta Charlie from Erub Island, a proud dancer with the Kerkar Kus Dance Team, as they travelled more than 2,500km to represent the Torres Strait at this year’s Darwin Aboriginal Art Fair.

For many of our First Nations peoples, we don’t stand on our own. We carry our families, ancestors and community with us wherever we go. Every performance is more than dance; it’s a representation of the generations who came before us and those who will follow.

SALOIAS positions itself in a fluid territory between sculpture, object and material research.

Artist spotlight - Sue Fraser

Change of Location!

Studio # 4 
(instead of # 26 as per the printed brochure)

Sue Fraser works from her studio within a ‘big scrub remnant’ from which she accesses fallen timber and found clay working towards supporting a sustainable wood firing practice. 

Discovering the ‘Tang art of China as an AIR in Jingdezhen Sue developed ideas based on women horses and power.  

She utilises a symbolic decorative surface that ascribes a story to each piece. 
Sue makes a variety of functional, hand built and wheel thrown work, utilizing ash and making glazes to suit her firing processes where the results from the kiln are unique.  

Her practice is an ongoing exploration into body and surface influenced by flame.

Join us at Middle Pocket Pottery on Friday, 21 August for a workshop as part of the North Coast Mud Trail. Step behind the scenes and deepen your understanding of the ancient art of Anagama wood firing. Learn how our kiln is fired continuously for more than 100 hours, then take part in the rare opportunity of unpacking the kiln by hand as each one-of-a-kind piece is revealed.
Set on our hinterland property six minutes from Billinudgel, you’ll gain a deeper understanding of this time-honoured ceramic tradition and be among the first to view our collectives’ latest pieces - fresh from the fire 🔥 
10:00 am to 2:00 pm

Arquivo Aires Mateus is a space devoted to exhibitions and special events. For the third year, it is generously offered by Manuel Aires Mateus to host Lisbon Design Week main exhibition. Its founder, internationally acclaimed Portuguese architect Manuel Aires Mateus, bases his design philosophy on the exploration of volumes and shapes, with meticulous focus on the importance of voids and empty spaces. 

𝗔𝘁 𝗟𝗗𝗪‘𝟮𝟲
Arquivo Aires Mateus presents “Design, Feito À Mão”, a collective exhibition that explores the relationship between craftsmanship and contemporary design. The exhibition, curated by André Matos, Vasco Águas and Astrid Suzano, highlights practices where the hand remains essential to the creative process. The jar, one of the oldest objects produced by human cultures, is here used as the main object of inquiry, inviting the public to reinterpret this archetypal form. With kind support by sponsors and partners @cosentinocitylisboa, @banema.studio, @gandiablasco_official, @barreirosebarreiros and @elitisfrance

Feeling honoured to have my ceramic work featured in the window of @stewarts_menswear in Mullumbimby in the lead-up to the Mud Trail.

Gerry has owned and worked in Stewart’s for more than 40 years and is a true local icon. It’s a privilege to have my work displayed in such a much-loved part of our community.

This week you’ll also see work by @jennjohnstonceramics and @jacquisos . It’s great seeing local artists and independent businesses collaborating to celebrate the creativity and spirit of our vibrant Northern NSW town.

If you’re in Mullum, take a stroll past the window, and don’t forget to visit me at Studio 19 during the Mud Trail! #mudtrail2026 #jayceramics #ceramicartist #northernnsw #mullumbimby

MOR is not only a showroom for exhibitions, but also a cultural hub where aesthetics meet functionality. Housed in a former garage that was later transformed into a carpentry workshop, the showroom presents a well-curated selection of contemporary design pieces. 

𝗔𝘁 𝗟𝗗𝗪‘𝟮𝟲
The ALLAY Collection, designed by Daniel Schofield, follows a philosophy of minimalist forms and clean geometric lines, reflecting the designer’s intention to create objects that feel familiar, purposeful and long-lasting. In particular, the exhibition focuses on the ALLAY chair and the MIGO side table, making its Lisbon Design Week debut in an updated version.

Bombony is a Portuguese artist of Ukrainian origin based in Lisbon. With a background in architecture and a former working experience as a partner of creative studio Woometry, she now runs her own activity. 

𝗔𝘁 𝗟𝗗𝗪‘𝟮𝟲

Finished works will be juxtaposed with works in progress, offering a rare behind-the-scenes.

Country to Couture 
❤️💛🖤

For the last two nights, two sold-out shows of over 1800 attendees witnessed First Nations textiles, fashion and art collide in a colourful showcase of creativity from across Australia.

For the first time in Country to Couture’s eleven-year history, the runway took place beneath the open sky on Larrakia Country, gathered around one of Darwin’s oldest living landmarks.

Planted more than 140 years ago, this heritage-listed boab has stood through generations of change. Beneath its branches, fashion became more than a runway - it was a celebration of culture, creativity, community and continuity.

Huge congrats to everyone who took part in this incredible display of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander fashion, textiles, art and design. 🙌🏿

Featured Artist | Christine Puruntatameri

Christine Puruntatameri is an artist who comes from a family of artists, yet has carved out her own distinctive style. She works with the pwoja, a comb carved from ironwood, to create layered markings across canvas, bark, and more recently hand built ceramics. 

Christine is the daughter of renowned potter Eddie Puruntatameri and while her practice is grounded in tradition, her work speaks with an unmistakably individual voice. Using classic ochre colours of red, yellow, and white, she also builds rich layers of pwoja lines with mixed ochres, incorporating hues of pinks, greens, and yellows.

We are proud to spotlight Christine and celebrate her work as the Feature Artist from @munupiarts

Join Injalak Arts as part of the Public Program for their talk on Renewing Rock Art on Country. Learn directly from contemporary rock art practitioners, find out more about their work and Injalak Arts.

caption:
My first solo exhibition, Long Story Short, opens Thursday 13 August, and I’d love to see you there.

Books and reading have been a cornerstone of my life - as companions, as a way of connecting with others, and as a way of understanding the world. Working with clay has offered me much the same. In this honest, humble craft I have found connection, creativity and calm. Long Story Short began with a desire to bring these two loves together: to set words that have moved me into clay, giving them permanent form.

The pieces in this exhibition carry text drawn from literature that has stayed with me - lines about love and loss, friendship, nourishment, the passage of time, and the wonder of the natural world. Some quotations speak boldly to the reader; others are more subtle, inviting closer consideration.

Making is where I find calm, and reading is where I find meaning. My hope is that these pieces carry something of both.

Join me for the opening, 5–7pm Thursday 13 August at Station Street Co-op, Bangalow. The exhibition continues through to Wednesday 26 August.

And save the date - on Friday 21 August I’ll be joined by @caitlin_reilly_ for an artist talk, part conversation, part literary salon, as part of the @northcoastceramics Mud Trail. More details to come.

Many thanks to the delightful and talented @oliviakatzphotography for the photos and making me feel at ease in front of the camera

Country to Collection: A Practical Framework for First Nations Creative Collaboration

Ty Symonds of Ty Symonds Studio, an independent brand, product and creative strategy practice, brings over 20 years of senior design leadership experience at some of Australia's most recognised retailers. 

A regular attendee of the Darwin Aboriginal Art Fair, Country to Couture, and the NIFA, Ty brings a practitioner's perspective to how the design industry engages with First Nations artists. 

Having led one of Australia's most recognised First Nations brand collaborations, a two-year co-design process with Ngen'giwumirri artist Kieren Karritpul (@merrepenarts) that has been widely acknowledged as an example of best practice in the industry, Ty speaks from experience rather than theory. His session draws on real processes, real mistakes, and real relationships built over time.

Artist spotlight - Kat Shapiro Wood

Studio # 21

SAFIR has come into being alongside Kat Shapiro Wood’s art practice to share her long-held passions for the beauty and effectiveness of function and design, in a form that can nestle into one’s home and living, quietly and gracefully. 

Attention to sensory detail, economy of form and a sensitively refined craftsmanship resolve into objects that hope to elevate our day to day experience of living.

Featured Artist | Doris Bush

Doris Bush was born in Haasts Bluff/Ikuntji circa 1942 and was married to the late George Bush Tjangala, one of Papunya Tula Artists’ original shareholders. 

In the mid 1980’s the family went to live on an outstation at Nyunmanu in Doris’ mother’s Country out towards the WA/NT border. 

Doris continues to paint Nyunmanu and the traditional Tjukurrpa (Dreaming) of this place, Dingo Dreaming.

We are proud to spotlight Doris and celebrate her work as the Feature Artist from @tjupiarts ❤️

FEATURED ARTIST | SALLY (SHARLENA) ROWE

Papunya Tula Artists' Featured Artist Sally (Sharlena) Rowe was born in Mparntwe (Alice Springs) in 1986 and grew up in Walungurru (Kintore). The daughter of renowned artists Bundi Rowe Tjupurrula and Nancy Young Napanangka, Sally began painting with Papunya Tula Artists in 2022.As a child, Sally learned by watching her grandparents, Wintjiya Napaltjarri and Toba Tjakamarra, paint in the Papunya Tula Artists studio. Today, she paints Pinari and its associated Tjukurrpa (Dreaming stories), for which she holds custodial rights through her grandmother. Featured Artist | Troy Drill

Troy Drill (b. 1981) is one of Warmun's most exciting emerging artists.Painting with traditional ochre and bush grass, Troy's work reflects the landscapes, stories and cultural knowledge of his Country. His distinctive style brings Country, memory and Dreamtime stories vividly to life. Since beginning his artistic practice, Troy has quickly gained national recognition. In 2025, he was selected as a finalist in three prestigious art prizes, winning one, and has since been featured in multiple exhibitions and selected for Rising Star 2026.

Following a career-ending sports injury, Troy turned to painting, transforming this challenge into a powerful journey of cultural expression, healing and connection to Country. 

Discover more about this artist and explore their available works via @warmunart ✨

Studio # 26

Jo Norton is an artist based in the Northern Rivers of New South Wales, working on Bundjalung Country. 

Her practice includes small porcelain vessels, stoneware forms, and site-specific installations. 

Using contemporary forms, she produces a body of work that comes together through two approaches: one developed within her emerging wood firing practice at Middle Pocket Pottery and the other through alternative firing techniques.

caption:
FEATURED ARTIST | ALMA

Pormpuraaw Art & Culture Centre's Featured Artist Alma is a Thaayorre woman and Traditional Owner of the land on which the community of Pormpuraaw sits. Her totems are the emu and black duck, and her deep connection to Country is central to both her life and artistic practice.Growing up in Pormpuraaw, Alma learnt bush skills, cultural knowledge and traditions from her parents, aunts, uncles and extended family. Today, she continues to pass this knowledge on to the younger generations in her family.An accomplished artist, Alma works across ghost net sculpture, painting and printmaking, drawing inspiration from the bush, waterways and traditions of Thaayorre country. 

Discover Alma's work at the 20th Darwin Aboriginal Art Fair this August on Larrakia Country.

Images courtesy of @pormpuraawartsandculturecentre.

@GapuwiyakCultureandArts is a remote Art Centre in East Arnhem Land, owned and governed by Yolŋu members through a Yolŋu Board. The Art Centre employs a manager and arts workers, supporting more than one hundred artists from Gapuwiyak and the surrounding homelands.

Gapuwiyak is a small Yolŋu community located in the Miyarrka region around Arnhem Bay. Eighteen clans are connected to this region, each with their own clan estates, songs, patterns and designs that continue to inform contemporary cultural and artistic practice.

The Art Centre supports artists to collect and prepare materials, create high-quality artworks, explore ideas, and develop cultural knowledge and artistic skills. It also assists with exhibiting, marketing and selling artworks both nationally and internationally.

In addition to its arts program, Gapuwiyak Culture and Arts runs tourism and cultural initiatives, offering visitors a welcoming place to meet, relax, enjoy a coffee and learn about Yolŋu culture and art.

ERAM é DJ, produtora e curadora, com um trabalho que transita entre a pista contemporânea, a cultura do soundsystem e a música eletrônica underground.  A frente de projetos como a RAJADA e residente da TIJOLO Records, ERAM carrega mais de uma década de envolvimento com cenas musicais underground. Ao longo desse percurso, desenvolveu uma abordagem singular que conecta tradições locais de pista a sonoridades globais da música de club. A partir de anos de pesquisa por diferentes culturas musicais, seus sets transitam com fluidez entre jungle, breaks, dub, grime, UK funky, garage, baile funk, bubbling, house e a música contemporânea de pista, guiados por narrativa, tensão e profundidade emocional, em vez de convenções rígidas de gênero.  Seja atrás dos toca-discos, no estúdio ou por meio de seu trabalho de curadoria, ERAM continua construindo conexões entre cenas, sonoridades e comunidades, aproximando diferentes tradições da música de pista a partir de uma perspectiva moldada pela cultura rave, pela herança dos soundsystems e por uma profunda crença no poder da experiência coletiva.

Clifford Thompson Japaljarri is a Kaytetye artist and a leading member of Tennant Creek Brio.His rhythmic repetitions and precise geometries create quiet, meditative works, where painting becomes an act of focus and care. Working across canvas, found metal and ceramics, Clifford's practice reflects a deep commitment to material, process and form.

His work has been exhibited at ACCA, NAP Contemporary, Cassandra Bird and Tolarno Galleries, and is held in major public collections including the Powerhouse, AGNSW and QAGOMA.

This year marks a special milestone: the 20th anniversary of the Darwin Aboriginal Art Fair — two decades of championing First Nations artists and Art Centres and celebrating the extraordinary cultural wealth they share with the world.

Produced in partnership with @ArtCollectorMagazine, this special edition features the artists and goings on at the Fair, plus analysis on important issues affecting the Indigenous arts industry.

This year's cover features Awareness XXII, 2025 by Solomon Booth from @Moa_Arts.

Inspired by the beautiful surroundings of his island home on Moa Island in the Torres Strait, Solomon's works draw upon Torres Strait and Melanesian influences. A founding Committee member and long-term Chairperson of Moa Arts, "Solly" is considered the backbone of the Art Centre, with a practice inspired by his ancestors' storytelling traditions and master craftsmanship.

Featured Artist | Janet Bromley 

Janet Bromley is a Yorta Yorta artist whose weaving practice sits at the intersection of cultural knowledge, environmental awareness, and contemporary storytelling. 

Her work is grounded in traditional Aboriginal methods of gathering and weaving yet reimagined through the use of non-traditional materials. Strips of fabric, fragments of plastic, wire, and organic fibres are layered and intertwined, creating textured surfaces that echo Country- its colours, rhythms, and histories. 

Through these materials- many once used and discarded- she explores themes of displacement, resilience, and the ongoing impact of consumerism on both people and environment. 

By reclaiming waste and reworking it through slow, deliberate processes, weavings becomes both an act of cultural continuation and a quiet form of environmental activism.

We are proud to spotlight Janet (@myarttime) and celebrate her work as the Feature Artist from @balukarts ❤️

Get ready to follow the mud trail! 
Every one of my bowls begins the same way—with hand-rolled coils of clay. No shortcuts, just a slow, rhythmic process that sets the pace for each unique piece.
But here’s the twist... I don’t build my bowls the usual way. I start upside down, beginning with the rim and gradually working my way to the base. It might look a little unconventional, but that’s part of the magic!
Come and watch the transformation unfold at my live bowl-making demonstration.
📍 Studio No. 10, Federal 📅 Saturday 22 August only 🕚 11:00 am
Come curious, stay inspired, and see how a handful of clay becomes a one-of-a-kind bowl before your eyes!

For 20 years, Darwin Aboriginal Art Fair has been more than an art fair. It has been a place where Culture is celebrated, communities come together, and First Nations artists lead the conversation.

For Executive Director Claire Summers, the impact extends beyond the event itself:
"One of the most incredible impacts of our events is how we cultivate community... There is such power in bringing people together in this inclusive environment."

From artists connecting with one another, to emerging creatives seeing what's possible, DAAF Foundation continues to create spaces where First Nations voices, creativity and leadership thrive.

As Artistic Director Simon Carmichael reflects: "When they come to the fair, they can see artists, stories and communities reflected back to them and hopefully feel inspired to share their own voice and creativity."

Through music, dance and storytelling, audiences are invited to experience Culture in ways that deepen their connection to the artworks, the artists and the communities represented across the fair.

"Cultural performances are part of the world's oldest continuing culture. Since time immemorial, song and dance has carried connection to Country, knowledge and story, passing these traditions from one generation to the next."

Thank you to writer Dr Diana Carroll for having a yarn, and DAAF media partner ArtsHub for highlighting the enduring impact of Darwin Aboriginal Art Fair 🖤

Detailed artistry from Michelle Pulatuwayu Woody Minnapinni, shortlisted for the NIFA Traditional Adornment Award, supported by Desart 🖤 

"Parmijini and all ceremonial ornaments are really important for when we have sorry business. We wear ornaments to help disguise ourselves from the deceased, as part of saying our last goodbye and letting them go, to help prepare them for the next journey. 
Only Tiwi make these ceremonial ornaments, because it is different to the mainland and we have different cultures in different places in Australia. These ornaments were passed on to us from our ancestors. 
Purukupali made the first Pukumani ceremony for his son Jirnani. His son was the first Tiwi person to die and he said ‘my son has passed away so we as Tiwi must follow my son and nobody is to live forever.’ 
Old people used to use [Tunga] to carry water. When they go out on Country, they use it to collect bush tucker, like mussels, fish, seashells, possums, bandicoot. They also used to collect yams in the Tunga.
They would use Tunga to carry their children on their shoulders or on their back. They also used Tunga during the Pukumani ceremony... It was for the deceased person’s belongings. No one is allowed to touch their stuff, especially those mob of the person who passed away. Otherwise, they might have a bad curse, they’ll get sick. Tunga was used for Pukumani ceremony, they would put it on top of the Pukumani pole."
- Michelle Pulatuwayu Woody Minnapinni, speaking on the cultural significance of her adornments of Tunga (bark basket) and Parmijini (headband/armbands).

How amazing are @IkuntjiArtists! Shortlisted for this year's NIFA Business Achievement award, supported by @CanberraCentre 🖤 

Founded in 1992, Ikuntji Artists was the first Art Centre established by women in the Western Desert Art movement. Since 2005, it has evolved from a community hub into a global powerhouse in fine art and fashion, championing Indigenous cultural sovereignty through commercial excellence.

"Innovation is our heritage". As the first Art Centre to transform traditional paintings into fabric designs, Ikuntji Artists has helped revolutionise the Indigenous textile movement. Today, through Ikuntji Designs, artist-led textiles and fashion bridge remote community tradition with global fashion, creating sustainable pathways for cultural expression while maintaining the integrity of artists' stories and connection to Country.

More than art, Ikuntji Artists supports community, creates sustainable income for artists, and documents Western Desert culture for future generations through artist-led storytelling, language, and multimedia.

Narelle has made the 800km journey from Kalkaringi to Garramilla/Darwin many times before as one of Karungkarni Art & Culture’s most seasoned DAAF participants.

But what she brought home from DAAF wasn’t something she could pack in the troopy.

Last year, Narelle became fascinated by DAAF’s Online Portal, learning how artwork sales are processed and connecting with customers who wanted to learn more about the stories behind the artwork.

For Karungkarni, it was their first experience selling artwork online. For Narelle, it was a chance to build practical skills, confidence and knowledge she could take home and share with community.

“At the end of the day it's just human connection. Sharing stories and knowledge.” – Nicole, Karungkarni Art Centre Manager

That’s what makes DAAF so special.
It’s a place where artists and Arts Workers can build connections, gain valuable skills and return home with opportunities that continue to grow long after the journey ends.

This EOFY, help make the next journey possible.
Your donation to the DAAF Travel Appeal helps artists and Arts Workers from remote First Nations communities travel to DAAF, share culture, generate income and bring knowledge home to strengthen their Art Centres and communities.

“The Darwin Aboriginal Art Fair is more than a three-day event. Long before the crowds arrive and long after they leave, DAAF Foundation brings together a national community connected by First Nations arts and culture. Through conversations, mentorship, cultural exchange and connections with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art Centres and creatives nationwide, we create space to share knowledge, build relationships and spark new collaborations. 

The strength of DAAF Foundation lies not only in the exchanges that take place during the Art Fair itself, but in the networks, relationships and mutual support that continue long after it ends. Increasingly, these connections extend nationally and internationally, working alongside communities and creating pathways for the next generation to continue keeping culture strong, learning from those who came before them.

The invitation is open and ongoing: stay connected and support Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art Centres and creatives throughout the year.” - Simon Carmichael, Artistic Director, Darwin Aboriginal Art Fair Foundation

Thank you for celebrating 20 years of strong Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander arts and cultures at DAAF with us.

Thank you to all of our partners and supporters for making DAAF 2026 possible.

Thank you to everyone who came down to the Darwin Convention Centre, hopped online, and bought a piece of art.

Richard started on the wheel in 1975 but became sidetracked by becoming involved in campaigning for animals and the environment and starting a mail order business.

He was elected to the Upper House of the NSW Parliament and his term ended in 2003.

Nyungawarra Ward Napurrula is a Ngaatjatjarra artist who was born near Karrku, east of Karrkurritinytja (Lake Macdonald), around 1956.

Based in Warakurna, Western Australia, Nyungawarra is known for her vibrant paintings of her ancestral Country, particularly the Patjarr region. Working in the Western Desert painting tradition, she creates intricate compositions that reflect the stories, landscapes and cultural knowledge of her homelands. Her works have been exhibited widely and are held in collections across Australia.

Making Plates – From Wheel to Mould
Many moons ago, while studying ceramics at TAFE, I threw a few plates on the pottery wheel. Those original plates became the foundation for what I do today, as I used them to create a mould that now helps me make consistent plates from slabs of clay.
The process begins with preparing the clay. A block of clay is cut and fed through the slab roller, which compresses and flattens it into an even sheet. The surface is carefully smoothed before the clay is cut to the required size.
The clay slab is then placed over the mould and gently pressed into shape. After smoothing the surface again, the excess clay is trimmed away. None of these offcuts go to waste—they are wedged and recycled for future projects.
Once the plate has firmed up to the right consistency, I stamp my maker’s mark into the base. The final stage at this point is refining the rim, carefully smoothing and shaping the edge to create a clean, professional finish before the plate continues through the drying and firing process.
It’s a method that combines traditional pottery skills with the efficiency of mould-making, allowing each plate to be both handcrafted and consistent in form.

“This is one of our biggest events that we drive quite a long way to participate in.” 🚗💨

Every year, artists from Karungkarni Art & Culture make the 9-hour journey from Kalkaringi to Garramilla/Darwin for DAAF. From flat tyres and corrugated roads to buffalo and kangaroos crossing the highway, every trip comes with its own challenges and surprises.

Last year, one of Karungkarni’s youngest artists, Kyliah Herbert, made a last-minute decision to jump in the troopy and join the journey.

What started as a spontaneous choice became a life-changing experience. 

Kyliah embraced every moment — sharing her culture and artwork, meeting hundreds of new people, building confidence, learning new skills, and discovering what DAAF can be for young artists.

These are the moments that often go unseen, but they are what make DAAF so special.

DAAF is about more than selling and buying art. It’s about creating opportunities for artists to grow their pride, confidence and connection.

Attend a local NAIDOC event. Watch a dance performance. Visit an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander art exhibition. Support Indigenous artists, designers and businesses. Listen to local Elders. Learn about the Country on which you live. Every conversation, every connection and every act of listening helps strengthen understanding and celebrate the richness of First Nations cultures.

Because NAIDOC has always been more than a week.
It is a celebration of survival.
A recognition of truth.
A continuation of culture.
A commitment to future generations.

At DAAF Foundation, we are honoured to work alongside Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander artists, designers, art centres and communities every day, creating spaces where culture leads, creativity flourishes, and First Nations voices are celebrated on their own terms.

As we honour 50 Years of Deadly, we celebrate every story that has brought us to this moment and look forward to the stories still waiting to be told.

Still Deadly. Always.
